Naturel doubles the l before -ment, heureux goes through the feminine heureuse, and franc through franche. Apparent follows the -ent → -emment rule, so the spelling has e but the sound is amment.
Adjectives ending in a vowel just add -ment: parfaitement, certainement, finalement, également, immédiatement. Évident is the trap: -ent becomes -emment, spelled with e but pronounced like amment.
These build on the feminine form: douce, sûre, complète and lente all give the adverb. Seul and exact are already vowel-final in sound, so seulement keeps the e while exactement simply adds -ement.
gentil forms its adverb irregularly: gentiment, with no l before the ending.

cards.de: I often go to the cinema.
cards.note: Unlike English, French never puts the adverb between the subject and the conjugated verb. It goes after the verb.
Short adverbs like bien, mal, déjà and souvent sit between the auxiliary and the past participle in compound tenses.
récent → récemment. Longer adverbs in -ment usually come after the participle or at the start of the sentence.

cards.fr: Il répond à nos questions avec patience.
cards.task: Replace the avec phrase with an adverb in -ment.
cards.answer: Il répond patiemment à nos questions.
accept: Il répond à nos questions patiemment.
cards.note: patient → patiemment. French often prefers an adverb in -ment to avec plus a noun.

cards.de: She has always loved the sea.
cards.note: toujours is a short adverb, so it goes between the auxiliary and the participle, not before the auxiliary.
The pronoun goes before the auxiliary. The participle agrees with a direct object that comes before it: vue.

cards.task: Both pronouns, in the right order
cards.note: Watch the switch: me, te and nous come before le, la, les (me le, te les, nous en), but lui and leur come after them (le lui, la leur), and en always sits last. The imperative Rends-le-moi flips everything: the object goes after the verb and me becomes moi.

Aider and connaître are direct (aide-le, je ne la connais pas), whereas répondre à, offrir à and dire à quelqu'un force lui/leur. Note that les covers the feminine photos too, since direct plural has one form for both genders.

Voir, écouter and attendre take a direct object (le, la, les), while téléphoner à, parler à and demander à quelqu'un need lui or leur. English pushes you the wrong way here: "phone her" looks direct, but French says je lui téléphone.
aider qn takes a direct object, so the pronoun is le, la or les, never lui.
téléphoner à qn takes an indirect object, so lui or leur. The same goes for répondre à qn and parler à qn.

cards.de: I'm waiting for him outside the cinema.
cards.note: attendre qn takes no preposition, so the pronoun is direct: le, la, les. Before a vowel, le becomes l'.

cards.fr: Je les ai dit la vérité.
cards.answer: Je leur ai dit la vérité.
cards.note: In dire quelque chose à quelqu'un the person is the indirect object, so leur. The thing said stays the direct object.

cards.task: Turn this into an affirmative imperative.
cards.note: In the affirmative imperative the pronouns follow the verb, direct object before indirect, and me becomes moi.
In the negative imperative the normal order before the verb comes back: me before le.
Both pronouns stay together in front of the auxiliary, and ne ... pas wraps around the whole group.

cards.de: Can you explain it to them?
accept: Est-ce que tu peux le leur expliquer ?
cards.note: With two verbs the pronouns go directly before the infinitive, not before the conjugated verb.

cards.de: I sent them to him (the letters).
cards.note: le, la, les always come before lui and leur. The participle agrees with the preceding les: envoyés.

cards.answer: Je lui ai téléphoné hier soir.
cards.note: téléphoner à qn is indirect, so the pronoun is lui. That is also why the participle shows no agreement.
croire qn takes a direct object, so la, never lui. The same goes for écouter qn and regarder qn.

cards.de: I'm going to give it to her tomorrow.
cards.note: After aller or vouloir plus an infinitive, the pronouns hang on the infinitive, in the order le before lui.
The person meant is him, so lui. In the affirmative imperative the direct object le comes first, then lui.

cards.de: Are you going to Paris? Yes, I'm going there tomorrow.
cards.fr: Tu vas à Paris ? Oui, j'___ vais demain.
cards.note: y replaces à plus a place (there) and à plus a thing (about it, on it): J'y pense.
S'intéresser à, participer à and croire à give y, while se souvenir de, avoir envie de and the quantity deux pommes give en. Croire à une histoire is the one learners miss and say en.
Y stands in for à plus thing (penser à, aller à, répondre à), en for de (parler de, avoir besoin de). The tricky one is la gare with revenir: you come back from a place, so it is en, not y.

cards.de: Do you want some bread? Yes, I want some.
cards.fr: Tu veux du pain ? Oui, j'___ veux.
cards.note: en replaces de plus a thing and quantities (some, of it). English often leaves it out, French never does.

cards.de: I don't feel like it any more.
cards.note: The verb is avoir envie de qc, so en stands for the "it". ne ... plus = not any more.

cards.de: How many brothers do you have? I have two.
cards.fr: Tu as combien de frères ? J'___ ai deux.
cards.note: With numbers and quantities en is compulsory in French, even though English just says "I have two". So never "J'ai deux" on its own.

cards.de: Are you thinking about the exam? Yes, I'm thinking about it.
cards.fr: Tu penses à l'examen ? Oui, j'___ pense.
cards.note: penser à qc needs y, because y stands for à plus a thing. With people you say instead je pense à lui.

cards.de: I'm talking to him about it.
cards.note: When two pronouns meet, y and en always come last: lui en, m'en, nous y. The order is me/te/lui/nous + y + en.

accept: Il n'y en a plus du tout.
cards.note: In il y a, en slips in between y and a. The negation wraps the whole group: ne ... y en a ... plus.

cards.de: There are a lot of them in this neighbourhood.
cards.answer: Il y en a beaucoup dans ce quartier.
accept: Dans ce quartier, il y en a beaucoup.
cards.note: il y en a is the set phrase for "there are some of them". Quantity words like beaucoup, trop, assez follow it.
s'habituer à qc needs y, not en. Only verbs built with de take en, for example se souvenir de qc: je m'en souviens.
In the passé composé, y and en go before the auxiliary, not after the participle. They can never sit at the end of the sentence.
In the affirmative imperative the tu form keeps its s before y and en: vas-y, manges-en, penses-y. The s is purely for the sound.

cards.de: Don't worry, my brother is going to take care of it tomorrow.
cards.fr: Ne t'inquiète pas, mon frère va ___ demain.
cards.note: s'occuper de quelque chose becomes s'en occuper with en. In a full sentence: Je m'en occupe demain.

cards.de: I have to think about it.
cards.note: With two verbs, the pronoun goes right before the infinitive it belongs to. réfléchir à qc becomes y réfléchir.
The number stays at the end of the sentence. The participle never agrees with en, so acheté keeps no s.

cards.de: Do you come from Lyon? Yes, I come from there.
cards.fr: Tu viens de Lyon ? Oui, j'___ viens.
cards.note: en also replaces de plus a place, so the place you come from. y is for the destination: j'y vais.

cards.de: Are you coming to my place?
cards.note: After a preposition you need the stressed forms: chez moi, avec toi, pour lui, sans elle.

After prepositions like avec, chez, sans and pour, use the stressed forms lui and elle, not il or elle as subject, and eux for a group of men. Note that nous and toi look the same as the ordinary subject pronouns, which is why the emphatic use at the start of a sentence is easy to miss.

cards.de: He's the one who is always late.
cards.fr: C'est ___ qui arrive toujours en retard.
cards.note: After c'est you always use the stressed pronoun: c'est moi, c'est toi, c'est lui. il cannot go there because it is a subject pronoun.

cards.fr: ___, je ne trouve pas ça drôle.
cards.hint: stressed pronoun at the start of the sentence
cards.note: For emphasis, put the stressed pronoun in front and still keep the subject pronoun: Moi, je... / Toi, tu... / Lui, il...

cards.de: She is taller than I am.
cards.answer: Elle est plus grande que moi.
accept: Elle est plus grande que moi !
cards.note: After que in a comparison French uses the stressed pronoun, so que moi and never que je.

cards.de: We are going to their place this evening.
cards.fr: Nous allons chez ils ce soir.
cards.answer: Nous allons chez eux ce soir.
cards.note: The stressed form of ils is eux, while elles stays elles. After prepositions like chez, avec or pour, ils is never possible.

cards.fr: Donne-___ le livre, s'il te plaît !
cards.note: In the affirmative imperative, me and te become moi and toi: donne-moi, lève-toi. In the negative imperative it stays ne me donne pas.

cards.de: My sister and I are going to Lyon.
cards.fr: Ma sœur et ___, nous allons à Lyon.
cards.note: With two subjects, French links them with the stressed form and sums them up with nous: ma sœur et moi, nous... je never follows et.
With -même you use the stressed pronouns: moi-même, toi-même, lui-même, elle-même, nous-mêmes, eux-mêmes.
Ownership is often expressed with être à plus a stressed pronoun: c'est à toi, ce sac est à elle.

cards.fr: Je vais au cinéma avec Pierre et Luc.
cards.task: Replace Pierre et Luc with a stressed pronoun.
cards.answer: Je vais au cinéma avec eux.
accept: Je vais au cinéma avec eux !
cards.note: After a preposition, people are replaced by the stressed form: avec eux for several men or a mixed group, avec elles only for women.
When the pronoun stands alone, with no verb, it must be the stressed form. je only exists directly before a verb.

cards.de: I'm the one who is right.
cards.note: After c'est moi qui, the verb agrees with the stressed pronoun: c'est moi qui ai, c'est toi qui as, c'est nous qui avons.

cards.de: The man whose car was stolen.
cards.fr: L'homme ___ la voiture a été volée.
cards.note: dont replaces de plus a noun, covering whose and of which. Also: le livre dont j'ai besoin.
Dont appears twice because both avoir besoin de and être fier de contain de. Où covers time as well as place here: le jour où we moved, alongside le restaurant où we eat.
Qui has a verb right after it (parle, part), que has a subject after it (je lis, nous avons vu). Parler de cette chose becomes dont, and la ville where you were born takes où, not que.
ce qui is the subject and is followed straight by the verb. ce que is the object and is followed by a subject: Ce que je veux, c'est partir.
où works for place and also for time: le jour où je suis né.
After a preposition you use lequel/laquelle/lesquels. With à and de they merge: auquel, duquel.

cards.de: The woman who lives next to us is a doctor.
cards.fr: La femme ___ habite à côté de nous est médecin.
cards.note: qui is the subject of the relative clause, so a verb follows it directly. It is used for people and for things.

cards.de: The film (that) I saw yesterday was boring.
cards.fr: Le film ___ j'ai vu hier était ennuyeux.
cards.note: que is the direct object, so a subject follows it. After que, a participle with avoir agrees with the noun it refers back to: la lettre que j'ai écrite. Unlike English, que can never be left out.

cards.de: I don't know what is happening.
cards.fr: Je ne sais pas ce que se passe.
cards.answer: Je ne sais pas ce qui se passe.
cards.note: Here what is the subject of se passer, so you need ce qui. ce que must always be followed by its own subject.

cards.de: The topic (that) we talked about is difficult.
cards.fr: Le sujet ___ nous avons parlé est difficile.
cards.note: Verbs that take de require dont: parler de, avoir besoin de, se souvenir de, rêver de.

cards.de: What I need is a bit of peace and quiet.
cards.fr: ___ j'ai besoin, c'est d'un peu de calme.
cards.note: When the verb takes de, the open what becomes ce dont. So Ce dont j'ai envie, not ce que j'ai envie.

cards.de: The problem (that) I am thinking about is serious.
cards.fr: Le problème ___ je pense est grave.
cards.note: à + lequel contracts to auquel, à + laquelle stays à laquelle, à + lesquels becomes auxquels.

cards.de: That's the park (that) I live opposite.
cards.fr: C'est le parc en face ___ j'habite.
cards.note: After prepositions containing de, such as en face de, à côté de, près de, you need duquel, de laquelle, desquels. Plain dont is not possible here.

cards.de: I remember the day we met.
cards.fr: Je me souviens du jour quand nous nous sommes rencontrés.
cards.answer: Je me souviens du jour où nous nous sommes rencontrés.
cards.note: After time words like le jour, l'année, le moment, French uses où, never quand, even though English says when. quand is only a question word or a conjunction.

cards.answer: C'est tout ce que je sais.
accept: Voilà tout ce que je sais.
cards.note: After tout you always need ce que or ce qui: tout ce que je sais, tout ce qui est possible.

cards.de: The colleagues I work with are very nice.
cards.answer: Les collègues avec qui je travaille sont très sympathiques.
accept: Les collègues avec lesquels je travaille sont très sympathiques.
cards.note: With people, qui is the usual choice after a preposition. lesquels is also correct but sounds more formal. Note that French never puts the preposition at the end.

cards.fr: Voici le village. Je suis né dans ce village.
cards.task: Join into one sentence with a relative pronoun.
cards.answer: Voici le village où je suis né.
accept: Voici le village dans lequel je suis né.
cards.note: où replaces a place expression together with its preposition and is shorter than dans lequel.

cards.de: What I fancy is a weekend by the sea.
cards.fr: ___ j'ai envie, c'est d'un week-end à la mer.
cards.note: avoir envie de takes de, so you need ce dont. Ce à quoi is only used with verbs that take à, for example Ce à quoi je pense.

cards.de: Where are your keys? (speaking to several people, or formally)
cards.note: vos goes before a plural noun, votre before a singular one. Both cover your to several people and polite your to one person.
Idée, histoire and erreur are feminine but begin with a vowel or silent h, so they take mon, not ma. Chambre and question start with a consonant and keep ma, while clés is plural and takes mes.

Amie, école and adresse are all feminine, yet they take mon because they start with a vowel sound: French avoids ma before a vowel. Sœur and voiture keep ma, and parents takes mes for the plural regardless of gender.

cards.de: Is this your car? (speaking to several people, or formally)
cards.note: votre is used before any singular noun, masculine or feminine. The plural form is vos.

cards.de: This isn't my key, it's yours.
cards.fr: Ce n'est pas ma clé, c'est ___.
cards.note: la clé is feminine, so la tienne. The possessive pronoun agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.

cards.de: Which dress? The one I bought yesterday.
cards.fr: Quelle robe ? ___ que j'ai achetée hier.
cards.note: The forms are celui (m), celle (f), ceux (m pl), celles (f pl). They agree with the noun they point back to.

cards.de: These aren't our seats, they're theirs.
cards.fr: Ce ne sont pas nos places, ce sont ___.
cards.note: For several owners the pronoun is le leur, la leur, les leurs. In the plural there is no difference between masculine and feminine.
Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h you use cet. Otherwise it is ce (m), cette (f), ces (plural).

cards.de: My bike is broken, I'll take my brother's.
cards.fr: Mon vélo est cassé, je prends ___ mon frère.
cards.note: English my brother's or the one belonging to becomes celui de, celle de, ceux de, celles de. The pronoun can never stand alone; it needs de, qui, que or ci/là.

cards.de: Which jumper do you want? This one.
cards.note: le pull is masculine singular, so celui. Add ci for the nearer item and là for the further one: celui-là.
The French possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. chapeau is masculine, so it is son even though the owner is a woman.

cards.de: The children have done their homework.
cards.fr: Les enfants ont fait leur devoirs.
cards.answer: Les enfants ont fait leurs devoirs.
cards.note: leur goes before a singular noun, leurs before a plural one. les devoirs is plural, so leurs.

cards.de: These shoes are mine, not yours.
cards.answer: Ces chaussures sont les miennes, pas les tiennes.
accept: Ces chaussures-là sont les miennes, pas les tiennes.
Ces chaussures sont les miennes, et non les tiennes.
cards.note: chaussure is feminine and here plural, hence les miennes and les tiennes. This kind of pronoun always keeps its article.

cards.task: Replace the noun with a possessive pronoun.
cards.note: les livres is masculine plural, so les tiens. The determiner tes becomes the pronoun le tien, la tienne, les tiens, les tiennes.

cards.de: Which photos do you like best? The ones from the wedding.
cards.fr: Quelles photos tu préfères ? ___ du mariage.
cards.note: photo is feminine, so the plural form is celles. The demonstrative pronoun takes the gender and number of the noun it replaces.
Personne ne … means nobody, Rien ne … means nothing. The ne stays and pas drops out.
chaque is only used before a noun, while chacun stands alone as a pronoun. There is no plural form chacuns.
Before a noun it is always chaque. chacun/chacune replaces the noun: chacun reçoit un livre.
tout le monde is grammatically singular even though it means everyone, so the verb is est.

cards.de: You can ask anyone, everybody knows him.
cards.answer: Tu peux demander à n'importe qui, tout le monde le connaît.
accept: Tu peux le demander à n'importe qui, tout le monde le connaît.
Vous pouvez demander à n'importe qui, tout le monde le connaît.
cards.note: n'importe qui means anyone at all, no matter who. After demander the person takes à.

cards.de: We can meet anywhere, I don't mind.
cards.fr: On peut se retrouver ___, ça m'est égal.
cards.note: The n'importe family uses question words: qui (who), quoi (what), où (where), quand (when), comment (how).
When rien or personne is the subject, ne still has to stand before the verb. Only pas disappears.
Verbs in -cer take a cedilla before o and a: nous commençons, je commençais. Without it, the c would sound like k.
Only the second é flips to è, and only when the ending is silent, so préfère and préfèrent contrast with préférons and préférez. The first é never moves.
The y stays only where the ending is pronounced, in payons and payez; elsewhere it becomes i. Note paient looks long but sounds exactly like paie.
Here the stem change is a doubled l rather than an accent: appelle in the four short forms, single l in appelons and appelez. Writing appèle is the usual slip.
The silent e of achet- becomes è whenever the ending is silent, so je, tu, il and ils all sound the same. Nous and vous keep the plain e because their endings are pronounced.

Only nous gets the cedilla: commençons keeps the soft s sound before o, while the e in commencez already does that job. The other four forms look identical in speech, since -e, -es and -ent are all silent.
The only form that changes is nous mangeons, where the e is kept to stop the g from hardening before o. Je mange and il mange are spelled and pronounced identically, as are tu manges and ils mangent.

cards.de: I get up at six o'clock.
cards.fr: Je me léve à six heures.
cards.answer: Je me lève à six heures.
cards.note: The accent here leans the other way: e becomes è, not é. Same pattern in je me promène and il achète.
Verbs in -ayer allow both spellings: je paie or je paye. The form with i is more common today.

cards.de: We travel to Italy every summer.
cards.note: Voyager is also a -ger verb, so it keeps the e before o: nous voyageons. The form nous voyagions would be imparfait or subjonctif.
Verbs in -oyer and -uyer always change y to i before a silent ending: je nettoie, il envoie, tu t'ennuies. But nous nettoyons.

cards.fr: Tu appelles ta sœur tous les soirs.
cards.answer: Vous appelez votre sœur tous les soirs.
cards.note: With nous and vous the ending is pronounced, so a single l is enough: nous appelons, vous appelez.

cards.de: Man braucht zwei Stunden, um dorthin zu kommen.
cards.fr: Il ___ deux heures pour y aller.
cards.note: falloir only exists impersonally: il faut. It covers English "you need", "you have to" and "it takes".
The v of the stem disappears in the singular, so je suis, tu suis, il suit look bare, and je suis is spelled exactly like je suis from être. Only context tells you whether it means I am or I follow.
The i becomes y before the pronounced endings of nous croyons and vous croyez, while ils croient keeps the i and the ending is silent. Crois, crois, croit all sound the same.
Il prend keeps the d of the infinitive with no ending after it, while nous and vous drop it (pren-) and ils doubles the n (prennent). Je prends and tu prends sound identical to il prend.
Three stems in one table: vien- in the singular, ven- for nous and vous, and vienn- for ils. Je viens, tu viens and il vient all sound the same, so only the spelling of the ending tells them apart.
Three stems here: doi- in the singular, dev- for nous and vous, and doiv- for ils. The singular forms all sound the same, and ils doivent adds the pronounced v that je dois lacks.
Short sai- forms in the singular contrast with the fuller sav- of nous, vous and ils. Remember savoir is knowing a fact or a skill, while connaître is being familiar with a person or place.
The stem shifts from voi- in the singular and ils to voy- before the -ons and -ez endings. Ils voient sounds just like je vois, tu vois and il voit; only the writing tells them apart.
Same pattern as pouvoir: veu- in the singular, voul- for nous and vous, veul- for ils. Je veux and tu veux are identical, and the written x is silent.

The stem shifts between peu- in the singular, pouv- for nous and vous, and peuv- for ils. The x of je peux and tu peux is silent but must be written; in questions the special form puis-je is used instead.

je dis and tu dis are spelled and pronounced alike, and the s of the singular stays silent while dis- in disons and disent sounds like a z. The real trap is vous dites, with no -ez: only dire, être and faire do this.

Three different stems in one table: vai/va in the singular, the infinitive stem all- for nous and vous, and vont for ils. Note that vais, vas, va all sound the same, so only the pronoun tells you who is going.

The three singular forms sound identical, and vous faites (not faisez) plus ils font are the two forms learners get wrong most often. Nous faisons is the odd spelling: ai is pronounced like the e in le.
The infinitive stem av- shows up only in nous avons and vous avez; elsewhere it vanishes into ai, as, a, ont. Remember j'ai with the apostrophe, and keep il a apart from the preposition à.

No single stem survives here: suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont all go their own way, so this table is pure memorisation. Note vous êtes with its circumflex, one of only three verbs whose vous form ends in -es rather than -ez.
prendre loses the d in the plural: nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent with double n.
dire: je dis, tu dis, il dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils disent. Note that vous dites has no -ez.
Use connaître for knowing people and places. savoir is for facts and for clauses, as in je sais qu'elle vient.
faire is irregular: nous faisons, vous faites, ils font. The form faisez does not exist.

cards.fr: Il écrit un long message à sa famille.
cards.answer: Ils écrivent un long message à leur famille.
accept: Ils écrivent un long message à leurs familles.
cards.note: écrire takes the stem écriv in the plural: nous écrivons, vous écrivez, ils écrivent. The possessive also changes to leur.

cards.de: I have to go now, but I can come tomorrow.
cards.answer: Je dois partir maintenant, mais je peux venir demain.
accept: Je dois y aller maintenant, mais je peux venir demain.
Je dois partir maintenant, mais demain je peux venir.
cards.note: devoir and pouvoir come straight before the infinitive, with no à or de. je dois, je peux, je veux all end in -x or -s.

cards.de: My sister went to the market this morning.
cards.fr: Ma sœur ___ au marché ce matin.
cards.note: aller is one of the movement verbs that take être. With être the participle agrees with the subject: allée.

Ouvrir, offrir and souffrir all give -ert despite their -ir ending, which is the main thing to remember. Courir, tenir and recevoir take -u instead, and reçu needs the cedilla to keep the s sound before u.

Four take -u (lu, bu, cru, connu), and dû carries a circumflex only in the masculine singular to distinguish it from the article du. Écrit is the outlier with -it, matching the t you hear in the feminine écrite.

Pris, mis and suivi all end in a silent vowel or consonant, but note the spelling difference: pris and mis keep the s, suivi does not. Mort and né are the ones learners get wrong, since neither looks like its infinitive; vécu is the only -u form here.
The participle is the very short cru, with no accent and no extra letters. In writing, the first person contracts to j'ai cru, and cru stays unchanged because the auxiliary is avoir.
The participle is suivi with no extra consonant, and avoir means no agreement with the subject. Note the common sense j'ai suivi un cours, I took a course.
The participle is pris, short and unrelated to the infinitive ending, and with avoir it stays unchanged unless the object comes first (les clés que j'ai prises). Je becomes j'ai.
Venir takes être, so the participle agrees: venue for a woman, venus/venues in the plural. Never say "j'ai venu".

The participle dû keeps a circumflex only in this masculine singular form (the feminine is due, no accent). Followed by an infinitive it means either obligation or a guess: j'ai dû partir, il a dû oublier.
The participle is just su, short and with no circumflex (unlike dû). In this tense savoir often means found out at a precise moment: j'ai su la vérité hier.
The participle is the very short vu, nothing like the infinitive. With avoir it stays unchanged unless the direct object comes first: la photo que j'ai vue.
The participle voulu is invariable here with avoir, and j'ai voulu usually means I decided or I tried, not simply I wanted. In the negative it is stronger still: il n'a pas voulu = he refused.
The participle is just pu, two letters, unrelated to the infinitive ending. J'ai pu usually means "I managed to", a completed success, not a general ability.
The past participle is the short dit, not "disé", and it stays unchanged with avoir. In writing, je ai becomes j'ai.
Aller takes être, so the participle agrees: add an e for a woman and an s for a plural group. Note the accent on vous êtes.
The past participle fait is short and unpredictable from the infinitive, and it never adds a letter here because avoir is the auxiliary. Remember the elision: j'ai fait, not je ai fait.
Avoir is its own auxiliary, so the auxiliary and the participle look nothing alike: ai plus eu. Eu is pronounced like a simple u sound, the e is silent, and je becomes j'ai eu.
Even though être is the auxiliary for many verbs, it takes avoir with itself, and the participle été never agrees with anything. Note the elision: je ai is written j'ai été.

cards.de: I stayed at home all weekend.
cards.fr: J'ai resté à la maison tout le week-end.
cards.answer: Je suis resté à la maison tout le week-end.
accept: Je suis restée à la maison tout le week-end.
cards.note: rester forms the passé composé with être, not avoir. The same group includes aller, venir, partir and arriver.

cards.de: I lost my keys on the train.
cards.answer: J'ai perdu mes clés dans le train.
accept: J'ai perdu mes clefs dans le train.
cards.note: Regular re verbs form their participle in u: perdre, perdu; attendre, attendu.

cards.de: I read this novel in two days.
cards.fr: J'ai ___ ce roman en deux jours.
cards.note: The participle of lire is lu. lit is a present tense form and lisé does not exist.

cards.fr: Il boit un café au bureau.
cards.answer: Il a bu un café au bureau.
cards.note: The participle of boire is bu. Other short ones: voir, vu; croire, cru; vivre, vécu.
Reflexive verbs take être and the participle agrees with the subject: couchée. With a masculine subject it stays couché.

cards.de: The film was just starting when I arrived.
cards.fr: Le film ___ quand je suis arrivé.
cards.note: Verbs in -cer take a ç before a: je commençais, tu commençais, but nous commencions.

The y stem runs through the whole table because it comes from nous croyons. Nous croyions and vous croyiez carry both the y and the i of the ending, the only place where croire shows a double letter sequence like this.
The stem suiv- comes from nous suivons and never changes here. Careful with je suivais, which looks close to forms of être and suffit only in spelling; the v belongs to suivre.
Built on pren- from nous prenons, so the double n of ils prennent disappears completely. Nous prenions and vous preniez need the i of the ending even though it is barely audible.
The imparfait keeps the nous venons stem throughout, so vien- never appears here. Watch nous venions and vous veniez: the i is easy to drop when the present nous venons has none.
The stem stays dev- everywhere, so this is the calmest table for devoir. Je devais usually translates as I was supposed to or I had to, without saying whether it actually happened.
One steady stem sav- across all six forms, built on nous savons. Je savais often means I knew already, as opposed to the passé composé j'ai su, which means I found out.
Every form keeps voy-, so the trap is written rather than spoken: nous voyions and vous voyiez need both the y of the stem and the i of the ending, giving a double letter you barely hear.
One stem voul- throughout, so no veux forms here. Note that nous voulions and vous vouliez look exactly like the present subjunctive of vouloir; only the context tells them apart.
All six forms use pouv-, the stem you hear in nous pouvons, so the peux and peuvent shapes of the present never appear.
One stem dis- everywhere, pronounced with a z, so the odd vous dites of the present disappears and vous disiez behaves normally.
The imparfait is completely regular here: one stem all- throughout, taken from nous allons, with no trace of vais or vont. In writing, je shortens to j' before the vowel: j'allais.
Everything is built on fais-, including the trap from the present: faisais and faisait are pronounced with the sound of fe, not fè. The ils form faisaient sounds exactly like je faisais.
Built regularly on the nous avons stem av-, giving j'avais through ils avaient with the standard endings. Nous avions and vous aviez are the only two forms where you hear the i of the ending.
Once you have the stem ét-, être behaves like every other verb in the imparfait, and je élides to j'étais. The je, tu, il and ils forms all sound identical despite the four different spellings.

cards.de: When I was little, I often played football.
cards.fr: Quand j'étais petit, j'ai joué souvent au foot.
cards.answer: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais souvent au foot.
cards.note: Repeated habits in the past go in the imparfait. Watch for signal words like souvent, toujours, tous les jours.

cards.de: She had already been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
cards.answer: Elle attendait depuis une heure quand le bus est arrivé.
accept: Elle attendait depuis une heure quand le bus est arrivé.
Cela faisait une heure qu'elle attendait quand le bus est arrivé.
cards.note: With depuis, French uses the imparfait where English says had been waiting.

cards.fr: Il habite à Lyon et il travaille dans une banque.
cards.answer: Il habitait à Lyon et il travaillait dans une banque.
cards.note: Lasting states in the past go in the imparfait. Each stem comes from the nous form of the present.

cards.de: There were a lot of people in the street.
cards.fr: Il était beaucoup de monde dans la rue.
cards.answer: Il y avait beaucoup de monde dans la rue.
cards.note: English there was or there were is il y avait, never il était.

cards.de: I just wanted to ask you something.
cards.answer: Je voulais juste te demander quelque chose.
accept: Je voulais simplement te demander quelque chose.
cards.note: The imparfait of vouloir sounds more polite and tentative than je veux.

cards.de: When I arrived, the train had already left.
cards.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, le train ___ déjà parti.
cards.note: plus-que-parfait = auxiliary in the imparfait + past participle. partir takes être.
Imperfect of avoir plus cru, written j'avais cru in the first person. Use it for a belief you held before some other past moment: j'avais cru qu'il viendrait.
Only avais, avait, avions, aviez, avaient change; suivi stays fixed. It marks the earlier of two past actions: il avait suivi la route avant de s'arrêter.

The participle is short and irregular: pris, with no -u and no added ending in the masculine singular. Before the vowel you say and write j'avais pris, and the whole thing places one past event clearly before another.
Imperfect of être plus venu, with the same agreement as the passé composé (elle était venue). Je contracts to j'étais.
Keep the circumflex on dû in every line; only avais, avait, avions, aviez, avaient change. It reports an obligation that came earlier: elle avait dû rentrer avant minuit.

Avoir carries all the changes while su stays fixed; watch the one letter gap between nous avions su and ils avaient su. It marks knowledge that came before another past event: il avait su la nouvelle avant nous.
Only avoir is conjugated; vu stays put. Je avais and tu avais are spelled and sound the same, and in speech il avait vu and ils avaient vu are hard to tell apart.

Only the avoir part moves; voulu never changes. Watch the ear traps: avais voulu covers both je and tu, and il avait voulu sounds very close to ils avaient voulu, so the subject pronoun is what tells you.
Same tiny participle pu after the imperfect of avoir; avais, avait and avaient are homophones. Il n'avait pas pu venir means he had been unable to come earlier on.

Avais, avait and avaient are all pronounced the same, so context or spelling decides the person. Use it for what had already been said before another past moment: il avait dit before something else happened.
The imperfect of être carries the tense, and allé still agrees with the subject in gender and number. Compare étions and étaient, which are easy to confuse in writing.
Only the avoir part moves; fait stays frozen in all six persons. Use it for what had already been done before another past moment, as in il avait fait ses devoirs avant de sortir.
Only the imperfect of avoir moves; eu stays fixed. Note the stacked vowels in nous avions eu and ils avaient eu, and remember this tense means had had: j'avais eu une idée avant lui.

Imperfect of avoir plus the invariable été; watch nous avions été against ils avaient été, which sound different but are only one letter group apart in writing. Use it for a state that was already over before another past moment: il avait été malade avant le voyage.

cards.de: She told me that she had already seen this film.
cards.fr: Elle m'a dit qu'elle ___ ce film.
cards.note: The plus-que-parfait shows an action earlier than another past action. Short adverbs like déjà sit between the auxiliary and the participle.

cards.de: We had left before the end.
cards.note: Verbs of movement like partir build the plus-que-parfait with être in the imparfait. avions été would mean we had been.

cards.de: She had already gone out of the house.
cards.fr: Elle avait déjà sorti de la maison.
cards.answer: Elle était déjà sortie de la maison.
cards.note: With no object, sortir takes être and the participle agrees with the subject. Only with a direct object do you say elle avait sorti la voiture.

cards.fr: Je n'avais compris pas la question.
cards.answer: Je n'avais pas compris la question.
cards.note: The negation wraps around the auxiliary only: ne before it, pas right after, then the participle.

cards.de: If you had called me, I would have helped you.
cards.fr: Si tu m'___, je t'aurais aidé.
cards.note: In past unreal conditions, si takes the plus-que-parfait and the main clause takes the conditionnel passé. Never use aurais after si.

cards.de: He had forgotten his keys, so he couldn't get in.
cards.answer: Il avait oublié ses clés, donc il ne pouvait pas entrer.
accept: Il avait oublié ses clés, alors il ne pouvait pas entrer.
Il avait oublié ses clés, c'est pourquoi il ne pouvait pas entrer.
cards.note: The forgetting happens before the second action, hence the plus-que-parfait. The result goes in the imparfait or passé composé.

cards.de: The letters I had written arrived yesterday.
cards.fr: Les lettres que j'avais ___ sont arrivées hier.
cards.note: With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object that comes before the verb. Here que stands for les lettres, so écrites.

cards.fr: Elle s'est couchée tôt parce qu'elle était fatiguée.
cards.task: Put the first clause into the plus-que-parfait.
cards.answer: Elle s'était couchée tôt parce qu'elle était fatiguée.
cards.note: est becomes était and the participle stays the same. The agreement in couchée is kept.

cards.de: My sisters had already left when I called.
cards.fr: Mes sœurs étaient déjà ___ quand j'ai téléphoné.
cards.note: With être the participle agrees with the subject. mes sœurs is feminine plural, so parties.

cards.de: They had never told me about this problem.
cards.fr: Ils ne m'avaient ___ parlé de ce problème.
cards.note: Like pas, jamais sits between the auxiliary and the participle. The object pronoun m' stays right before the auxiliary.
The future stem of voir is verr-, not voir-.
The future goes back to croi-, so no y appears at all: croir- plus the endings. Note the two vowels in a row, je croirai, not je croyerai.
Drop the final e of suivre and you have the stem suivr-, identical for all six persons. Keep the v: suivrai, not suirai.
Unlike the present, the d stays in every form: the stem is simply prendre minus the final e, giving prendr-. Do not import the double n from ils prennent.
The future stem viendr- gains a d that is nowhere in the infinitive, and it stays the same for all six persons. Tenir and its family behave the same way.
The future drops the oi and uses devr-, with a single r, unlike voir's verr-. Note the past participle dû carries a circumflex, but nothing in the future does.
The future stem is saur-, with no v at all, so it sounds close to the future of être at times; compare je saurai with je serai and keep the two apart.
The future stem verr- drops the o of voir entirely and takes a double r throughout. Keep both r's, since a single one would give the unrelated verb verser style spellings and change the sound.

The future stem is voudr-, the same one you already know from the conditional je voudrais. Only the ending separates a polite je voudrais (I would like) from je voudrai (I will want), so listen for that final syllable.
The future stem has a double r, pourr-, which is clearly pronounced and separates je pourrai from the conditional je pourrais by just one letter.
Drop the final e of dire and you have the future stem dir-, so no surprises here. Careful not to confuse je dirai (future) with the imparfait je disais.
The future is built on a stem that appears nowhere else: ir-, with nothing left of aller. Endings are the standard ones, and je becomes j' before the vowel: j'irai.
The ai of faire drops out and the stem becomes fer-, so je ferai has nothing that looks like the infinitive. Same stem for the conditional (je ferais), so keep the final -ai and -ais apart.
The stem is aur-, not avoir-, so you get j'aurai, tu auras and so on. This is the stem you need for the futur antérieur (j'aurai fini), so it is worth drilling.
The stem is ser-, with no trace of être in it, and the same stem gives the conditional (je serais). Watch je serai versus je serais: one letter separates a promise from a maybe.

cards.de: When you arrive in Paris, call me.
cards.note: After quand, dès que and lorsque, French uses the future when the action is in the future. English uses the present here, so this feels odd at first.

cards.de: If I have time, I'll come.
cards.fr: Si j'aurai le temps, je viendrai.
cards.answer: Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai.
cards.note: After si meaning if, French uses the present, never the future. The future belongs in the main clause, just as in English.

cards.de: Tomorrow I will be able to help you.
cards.note: The future stem of pouvoir is pourr- with a double r. The same happens with courir → courr- and mourir → mourr-.
The future stem of devoir is devr-. The endings are always -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.
pleuvoir has the future stem pleuvr- and only exists in the third person singular.

cards.de: We will have to leave early.
cards.note: falloir becomes il faudra in the future. English uses a personal subject with "have to", while French prefers the impersonal il faut.

cards.de: I will send you a message this evening.
cards.fr: Je t'___ un message ce soir.
cards.note: envoyer has the irregular future stem enverr-, not envoier-.

cards.de: We will buy a new car next year.
cards.fr: Nous ___ une nouvelle voiture l'année prochaine.
cards.note: Verbs like acheter keep the accent grave in the future: j'achèterai. achèterions would be the conditional.

cards.fr: Je vais faire les courses demain.
cards.task: Change from futur proche to futur simple.
cards.note: The future stem of faire is fer-. The futur proche (aller + infinitive) sounds more conversational, the futur simple more neutral or written.

cards.de: Soon we will know the truth.
cards.note: The future stem of savoir is saur-. Do not confuse it with avoir → aur-.

cards.de: As soon as he arrives, we will eat.
cards.note: After dès que, French uses the future where English uses the present. Both verbs go into the future.
venir de + infinitive means to have just done something. aller + infinitive means to be about to do something.

Aller never moves; it is venir that carries the person, and de elides before the vowel: je viens d'aller, nous venons d'aller. Use it for a trip just completed, je viens d'aller à la poste, not for where you are now.

All six forms change only in venir, with the stem shift from vien- to ven- in nous venons and vous venez, then back to vienn- in ils viennent. Since faire starts with a consonant, de keeps its e: je viens de faire les courses.

Only venir is conjugated here; avoir stays in the infinitive. Watch the spelling trap: before a vowel de becomes d', so you write and say je viens d'avoir, il vient d'avoir (as in je viens d'avoir 20 ans, I've just turned 20).
Venir de carries the person and être stays in the infinitive. In writing, de elides before the vowel, so the forms are je viens d'être, il vient d'être, and so on.
Aller appears twice, once conjugated and once as the infinitive, which is correct French: je vais aller. In speech people often drop the second one and just say je vais à Paris.
Faire stays in the infinitive; all the change is in vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont. Common for weather and plans: il va faire froid, on va faire les courses.
Aller takes all the endings and avoir never changes shape. This is the usual way to give a future age or state: je vais avoir vingt ans.
Only aller carries the endings; être stays in the infinitive throughout. Very frequent with a subject like ça: ça va être long.

cards.de: We are going shopping in a moment.
cards.note: The futur proche is aller in the present plus an infinitive. It expresses a near or firmly planned future.
The passé récent is formed with venir in the present plus de plus an infinitive. There is no such thing as vont de.

cards.fr: Je téléphone à ma sœur ce soir.
cards.answer: Je vais téléphoner à ma sœur ce soir.
cards.note: Only aller is conjugated; the main verb stays in the infinitive. The present tense then becomes a near future.

cards.task: Express this with the passé récent.
cards.note: The passé récent replaces the passé composé when the action happened a moment ago. You do not need to add juste.

cards.de: I am not going out this evening.
cards.fr: Je vais ne pas sortir ce soir.
cards.answer: Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.
cards.note: With aller plus infinitive, ne ... pas wraps around the conjugated aller only. The infinitive follows afterwards.
Without de, venir plus infinitive means to come in order to do something. In the passé récent, de is obligatory.

cards.de: I will explain it to you in a moment.
cards.note: In the futur proche, object pronouns go directly before the infinitive, not before aller. le becomes l' before a vowel.

cards.de: She had just left the house when the phone rang.
cards.answer: Elle venait de quitter la maison quand le téléphone a sonné.
accept: Elle venait de sortir de la maison quand le téléphone a sonné.
cards.note: For "had just done something", venir goes into the imparfait: venait de plus infinitive.

cards.de: Tomorrow I'm going to the cinema.
cards.note: aller agrees with the subject: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons. The main verb stays in the infinitive.

cards.de: We're going to bed early tonight.
cards.note: With reflexive verbs the pronoun sits right before the infinitive and matches the subject: on va se coucher, nous allons nous coucher.

cards.de: When you get back, I'll have finished.
cards.note: The futur antérieur is the auxiliary in the future plus the past participle. It marks an action completed before a future moment.
Note the contraction j'aurai cru, and keep it apart from the conditional j'aurais cru: one written s is the only difference, and the two sound almost identical.
The stems aur- carry the whole tense and suivi never varies. Compare j'aurai suivi (will have followed) with the conditional j'aurais suivi: one s changes the meaning completely.
Only the auxiliary moves here; pris never changes. Watch the single letter that separates j'aurai pris (will have taken) from the conditional j'aurais pris (would have taken).
Future of être plus venu, used for something finished before another future moment: quand il sera venu, on commencera. Only one letter separates je serai venu from the conditional je serais venu.
Avoir in the simple future plus dû, with the circumflex kept throughout. Very often it is a supposition about the past: il aura dû rester au bureau.

Only the avoir forms move, and aurai (je) versus aura (il) differ by a single letter in writing and barely in sound. Besides future completion, it can express a guess: il aura su la réponse par un ami.
Compare aurai (je) with aura (il): one silent letter. This is the tense you need after quand or dès que for the earlier of two future events: quand j'aurai vu le film, je te dirai.

Note the bare aurai for je against aura for il, one silent letter apart. Beyond the plain time use, this tense often expresses a guess about the past: il aura voulu bien faire = he must have meant well.
Keep aurai apart from aurais: quand j'aurai pu lui parler points forward, not to a hypothesis. The participle pu never changes.
Watch aurai (future) against aurais (conditional); one letter separates "I will have said" from "I would have said". Note the elision in j'aurai dit.
Built on the future of être, whose stem ser- looks nothing like the infinitive. The agreement on allé continues to follow the subject.
Built on the future of avoir plus the fixed participle fait. Note the nous and ils forms of the auxiliary, aurons and auront, which sound alike but differ in writing.
Two forms of the same verb side by side: aurai eu, auras eu, aura eu. Distinguish j'aurai eu (future) from j'aurais eu (conditional); the s changes the meaning completely.

Future of avoir plus été, so the only thing that changes is the auxiliary: aurai, auras, aura, aurons, aurez, auront. Often used for a guess about the past: il aura été surpris, he must have been surprised.

cards.de: As soon as she has arrived, we'll start.
cards.note: arriver forms its compound tenses with être, hence sera arrivée. English uses the present perfect here, French uses the futur antérieur.

cards.de: After you have eaten, we'll go out.
cards.fr: Après que vous ___ mangé, nous sortirons.
cards.note: After après que, quand, dès que and lorsque, French uses the futur antérieur when the main clause is in the future. English just uses the present perfect or present.

cards.de: When we have got home, I'll call you.
cards.fr: Quand nous aurons rentrés à la maison, je t'appellerai.
cards.answer: Quand nous serons rentrés à la maison, je t'appellerai.
cards.note: rentrer is one of the être verbs, so it is serons rentrés, not aurons rentrés.

cards.de: She will have got up early.
cards.note: Reflexive verbs form the futur antérieur with être, and the participle agrees with the subject: levée.

cards.fr: Il finira son travail avant midi.
cards.answer: Il aura fini son travail avant midi.
cards.note: The futur simple finira becomes aura fini. The futur antérieur shows the action is finished before a point in the future.

cards.answer: Tu n'auras pas reçu ma lettre.
cards.note: In compound tenses ne and pas wrap around the auxiliary only, with the participle after them.

cards.de: By tomorrow evening we will have finished everything.
cards.answer: Demain soir, nous aurons tout terminé.
accept: D'ici demain soir, nous aurons tout terminé.
Demain soir, nous aurons tout fini.
D'ici demain soir, nous aurons tout fini.
cards.note: tout goes before the participle as an object pronoun: nous aurons tout terminé. English 'will have finished' matches the futur antérieur exactly.

cards.de: At ten o'clock the children will already be in bed.
cards.fr: À dix heures, les enfants se ___ déjà couchés.
cards.note: Reflexive verbs take être: se seront couchés. déjà goes between the auxiliary and the participle.

cards.de: He isn't here. He must have missed his train.
cards.fr: Il n'est pas là. Il ___ son train.
cards.note: The futur antérieur can also express a guess about the past, like English 'he must have missed'.

cards.de: I'll call you as soon as I have arrived.
cards.note: After dès que French uses the futur antérieur when talking about the future. arriver takes être.
The stem voudr- is the same as in the future (je voudrai). Conditionnel = future stem plus imparfait ending.

The stem is croir-, the infinitive minus its e, so the oi never turns into the croy- you see in nous croyons or the imperfect croyions. Watch the single letter gap between je croirais here and the future je croirai, which is what makes I would believe versus I will believe.

The stem is just the infinitive minus the final e, suivr-, so the v stays everywhere, unlike the present where je suis loses it. The four singular/third person forms all sound the same, and for nous and vous keep the r that separates this from the imperfect suivions, suiviez.
Only the final e of prendre drops, leaving prendr- for every person, so this is one of the most predictable stems here. The d is silent, and the r before the ending must not be lost in speech.
The stem viendr- takes the ie of the present je viens and adds d, so it looks nothing like the infinitive. The same stem serves all six persons.
The stem devr- loses the o of devoir, and these forms are the normal way to say should: tu devrais partir. Nous devrions and vous devriez keep the i before the ending.
The stem saur- drops the v of savoir entirely, so do not write saverais. Je ne saurais pas is a common way to say I wouldn't know how.
The stem verr- has a double r, unlike devrais or saurais, and the first vowel is written e though it sounds like è. Keep the extra i in nous verrions and vous verriez.
The stem voudr- adds a d that appears in no present form, and je voudrais is the polite way to ask for something instead of je veux. All persons keep the same stem.
The stem pourr- keeps a double r that you can hear lightly, and it is quite different from the present peux/peut. This is the standard way to soften a request: pourriez-vous répéter ?
The stem is just the infinitive minus e, so dir- plus the endings, with no change anywhere. Compare je dirais here with je dirai in the future: the written s is the whole difference.
Nothing of aller survives: the stem is simply ir-, and the je form is written j'irais with elision. Four forms sound alike, so context tells you which person is meant.

The infinitive faire loses its ai and shrinks to fer-, pronounced like the fe of fenêtre, so je ferais does not sound like faire. Watch nous ferions and vous feriez, where the i is easy to drop in writing.
The stem is aur-, with two r sounds only in the writing of pourrais, not here. Before a vowel the je form elides to j'aurais, and the singular forms plus ils are pronounced identically.

The stem ser- runs through all six persons, so the only work is the endings; je, tu, il and ils all sound the same despite the different spellings. Use it for polite or hypothetical statements, as in ce serait parfait.

cards.de: If I had time, I would do more sport.
cards.fr: Si j'avais le temps, je ___ plus de sport.
cards.note: After si you use the imparfait, and the conditionnel in the main clause. faire has the irregular stem fer-.

cards.de: If I were you, I wouldn't wait.
cards.fr: Si j'___ toi, je n'attendrais pas.
cards.note: The si clause never takes the conditionnel, only the imparfait. English 'if I were' is a past form here too.
The conditionnel makes requests more polite. English "could you" matches tu pourrais exactly.

cards.de: If I were you, I would go to the doctor.
cards.fr: À ta place, j'___ chez le médecin.
cards.note: Aller has the irregular stem ir-, giving j'irais. French uses one verb form where English needs "would go".

cards.de: Could you tell me the time?
cards.fr: Est-ce que vous pouviez me dire l'heure ?
cards.answer: Est-ce que vous pourriez me dire l'heure ?
cards.note: Polite requests need the conditionnel, not the imparfait. Vous pouviez would mean "you were able to" back then.
Devoir in the conditionnel gives advice and corresponds to English "should". The stem is devr-.

cards.de: If he had more money, he would buy a car.
cards.answer: S'il avait plus d'argent, il achèterait une voiture.
accept: Il achèterait une voiture s'il avait plus d'argent.
cards.note: Si becomes s' before il. Acheter keeps its accent in the conditionnel: il achèterait.

cards.de: If I were you, I would have said it.
cards.fr: À ta place, je l'___ dit.
cards.note: The conditionnel passé is the auxiliary in the conditionnel plus the past participle.
Written j'aurais cru in the first person, with the s that the futur antérieur lacks. J'aurais cru que... is the everyday way to say I would have thought that...
Aurais, aurait and auraient sound identical, so listen for the pronoun. Typical use is an unfulfilled past: j'aurais suivi ton conseil si tu me l'avais dit.
Aurais, aurait and auraient are pronounced alike, so the subject pronoun is your only clue in speech. This is the form for regrets and reproaches: j'aurais pris le train, tu aurais pris ton temps.

Conditional of être plus venu, for what would have happened: il serait venu si... The participle still agrees (elle serait venue), and the s in serais/serait is the only clue that this is not the futur antérieur.

This is the form for regret: j'aurais dû partir means "I should have left", always followed by an infinitive. Keep the circumflex on dû (it separates the participle from du), and note that with avoir it never adds an agreement ending here. Written out, je becomes j' before aurais.
This is the tense of si j'avais su: si j'avais su, je serais venu. Remember that aurais, aurait and auraient are homophones, so the subject pronoun is your only clue when listening.

The participle vu never changes here, so all the work is in avoir: aurais, aurais, aurait and auraient sound exactly alike, only the spelling differs. Write j'aurais vu with elision, and use it for things that did not happen: à ta place, j'aurais vu le film.
This is the polite regret form you will use most: j'aurais voulu vous aider = I would have liked to help you. Spelling is the only difference between aurais and aurait, since they sound the same.
J'aurais pu is the everyday way to say "I could have", often with regret, and it is followed by an infinitive: tu aurais pu me le dire. Aurais, aurait and auraient are pronounced alike.
Aurais, aurait and auraient sound identical, so only the ending in writing shows who is speaking. This is the form for things not said: j'aurais dit la vérité si...
The only difference from the futur antérieur is the extra i in the auxiliary, so serai allé and serais allé sound the same but say different things. Keep the agreement on allé.
The auxiliary looks almost identical to the futur antérieur but carries an extra i in every person. Use it for the thing you did not do: j'aurais fait autrement.
Aurais, aurais, aurait are pronounced the same, so the ending must be chosen from the subject alone. Classic use is the unreal past: j'aurais eu le temps si tu m'avais prévenu.

The trap is spelling in the singular: j'aurais/tu aurais with s and final t in il aurait, all sounding identical. Typical use is regret or unconfirmed news: ça aurait été mieux, or le témoin aurait été présent.

cards.de: If I had had time, I would have come with you.
cards.fr: Si j'avais eu le temps, je ___ avec vous.
cards.note: Venir is an être verb, so je serais venu. After si you use the plus-que-parfait, and the conditionnel passé in the main clause.

cards.de: If I had known, I would not have come.
cards.fr: Si j'aurais su, je ne serais pas venu.
cards.answer: Si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venu.
accept: Si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venue.
cards.note: A -rais form never follows si. An unreal condition in the past takes the plus-que-parfait: si j'avais su.
English "should have" corresponds to devoir in the conditionnel passé: j'aurais dû, tu aurais dû. An infinitive follows.

cards.answer: Nous aurions pu partir plus tôt.
accept: On aurait pu partir plus tôt.
cards.note: "Could have" is expressed with pouvoir in the conditionnel passé: j'aurais pu, nous aurions pu, plus an infinitive.

cards.fr: Si j'avais de l'argent, j'achèterais cette maison.
cards.task: Put into the past: si plus plus-que-parfait and conditionnel passé.
cards.answer: Si j'avais eu de l'argent, j'aurais acheté cette maison.
cards.note: An unreal condition about the present (imparfait plus conditionnel présent) becomes plus-que-parfait plus conditionnel passé when it refers to the past.

cards.de: The theft is said to have taken place during the night.
cards.fr: Le vol ___ eu lieu pendant la nuit.
cards.note: In news reporting the conditionnel passé marks information that is not confirmed. English uses "is said to have" or "reportedly".
With être as the auxiliary, the participle agrees with the subject: elles seraient parties.

cards.de: He said he would be finished before midnight.
cards.fr: Il a dit qu'il ___ fini avant minuit.
cards.note: In reported speech after a past verb, the futur antérieur becomes the conditionnel passé.

cards.de: Without you, I would never have managed it.
cards.answer: Sans toi, je n'y serais jamais arrivé.
accept: Sans toi, je n'aurais jamais réussi.
Sans toi, je n'y serais jamais arrivée.
cards.note: The conditionnel passé describes something that did not happen. The condition need not use si; here sans toi expresses it.
que je vienne, que tu viennes, que nous venions.

Two stems here: croi- for je, tu, il and ils, croy- for nous and vous. Watch the yi in croyions and croyiez, where the subjunctive i is added on top of the y; and note that je croie and il croie are spelled the same, with tu croies only adding an s.
The v comes back everywhere here, even in the singular: que je suive, unlike the indicative je suis. Nous suivions and vous suiviez carry an extra i and are identical to the imperfect.
The double n appears in prenne, prennes, prennent, while nous prenions and vous preniez keep a single n and match the imperfect exactly. Je prenne and il prenne are the same form.
The stem splits: vienn- with a double n in je, tu, il and ils, but the softer ven- in nous venions and vous veniez, which look exactly like the imperfect. Je vienne and il vienne are identical.

The stem splits in two: doiv- for je, tu, il and ils, but dev- for nous devions and vous deviez, which look identical to the imperfect indicative. Note that je doive and il doive are spelled the same.

The stem splits: voi- plus silent endings for je, tu, il and ils (voie and voient sound the same), while nous and vous keep voy-. The trap is the double letter in voyions and voyiez, which is what distinguishes them from the indicative voyons and voyez.
The stem stays dis- everywhere, so nous disions and vous disiez look exactly like the imperfect and differ from indicative nous disons. Dise, dises and dise are pronounced the same.
Two different stems in one table: aill- for je, tu, il and ils, but the regular all- returns for nous and vous. The je and il forms are spelled the same.

A completely separate stem sach- runs through the whole table, including nous and vous, where most verbs would go back to the nous form of the present. The same stem gives the imperative sache and sachez.

Two stems split the table: veuill- for je, tu, il and ils, but plain voul- for nous and vous, which look exactly like the imparfait forms voulions and vouliez. Note that je, tu and il sound identical despite the different spellings.

The subjunctive uses a stem of its own, puiss-, in all six persons, with no switch to pouv- for nous and vous. You need it after things like il faut que or bien que when saying someone is able to do something.
One clean stem fass- across all six persons, with the normal subjunctive endings. Use it after expressions like il faut que je fasse or bien que tu fasses.
The stem shifts from ai- in the singular and ils to ay- in nous ayons and vous ayez. J'aie, tu aies, ils aient all sound the same, and il ait ends in -t rather than the expected -e.

Two stems: soi- in the singular and ils, soy- before the -ons and -ez endings. Unlike almost every other verb, these endings are not the usual -e, -es, -e, so sois and soit have to be learned as they stand.

cards.de: Although he has the time, he isn't coming.
cards.fr: Bien qu'il ___ le temps, il ne vient pas.
cards.note: bien que always takes the subjonctif. From avoir: que j'aie, que tu aies, qu'il ait, que nous ayons.
Despite expressing a wish, espérer que takes the indicative. The subjonctif appears after wanting, doubt or emotion.

cards.de: I want to go to Paris.
cards.fr: Je veux que j'aille à Paris.
cards.note: When both clauses share the same subject, French uses the infinitive instead of que plus subjonctif.

cards.de: It's important that we're on time.
cards.answer: Il est important que nous soyons à l'heure.
accept: C'est important que nous soyons à l'heure.
Il est important que nous soyons ponctuels.
cards.note: Impersonal expressions of judgement such as il est important que, il est possible que and il vaut mieux que take the subjonctif.

cards.fr: Je ne crois pas qu'il ___ raison.
cards.note: Negated verbs of opinion such as ne pas croire que and ne pas penser que express doubt and take the subjonctif. In the affirmative: je crois qu'il a raison.

cards.answer: Il faut que tu fasses tes devoirs.
cards.note: devoir plus infinitive can be reworded as il faut que plus subjonctif. The subjonctif stem of faire is fass-.

cards.de: Although we left early, we arrived late.
cards.fr: Bien que nous ___ tôt, nous sommes arrivés en retard.
cards.note: bien que always takes the subjonctif. partir forms compound tenses with être, so soyons partis.
The whole tense rests on the subjunctive of avoir, so aie, aies, ait and aient all sound the same and only cru is stable. The first person contracts to j'aie cru.
Here the auxiliary is aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient, with four of them pronounced the same way. The participle suivi stays unchanged after avoir.

The auxiliary is the subjunctive of avoir: aie, aies, ait and aient all sound the same, while ayons and ayez keep no i before the ending. Use it after bien que, je doute que and similar when the taking already happened.
Subjunctive of être plus the agreeing participle venu. Sois, soit and soient are pronounced alike, so listen for the plural venus instead.
The whole table is subjunctive avoir plus the fixed participle dû, so aie, aies, ait and aient all sound the same and only spelling tells them apart. In writing, je shortens to j'aie.

The auxiliary takes its subjunctive shapes aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient, all silent-ending except the nous and vous forms. Expect it after expressions of feeling or doubt: je suis content que tu aies su répondre.
Four of the six auxiliary forms (aie, aies, ait, aient) are pronounced the same way, so listen to the subject, not the ending. Note j'aie vu with elision, and the y spelling in ayons and ayez.

Aie, aies and ait are pronounced alike, so only the ending on the page separates je, tu and il. It turns up after bien que or dommage que when the wanting is already over: dommage qu'il ait voulu partir.

The participle is just two letters, pu, so the whole weight falls on the subjunctive of avoir: j'aie pu, il ait pu and ils aient pu all sound identical. Use it for a completed possibility seen from now: je suis content qu'il ait pu venir.
The auxiliary forms aie, aies and ait are all pronounced like a simple è, and ayons/ayez are spelled with ay, no accent. Typical use: je ne crois pas qu'il ait dit ça.

Aller takes être here, so the participle agrees: allé with je, tu, il, and allés with nous, vous, ils (add an e for a female subject). Sois, soit and soient all sound identical, so only the spelling tells the persons apart.
The subjunctive of avoir is the trap here: il ait has no e, and the nous and vous forms are spelled with ay. Elision gives j'aie fait.
Aie eu, aies eu, ait eu all sound identical, and the repeated vowel sounds make it awkward to say. Use after que when the action is already completed: bien qu'il ait eu des difficultés.

Subjunctive of avoir plus été: aie, aies, ait sound exactly the same, and only nous ayons and vous ayez show the y. Use after expressions of emotion or doubt about something finished: je suis content que tu aies été là.

cards.de: I doubt he understood the question.
cards.fr: Je doute qu'il a compris la question.
cards.answer: Je doute qu'il ait compris la question.
cards.note: douter que takes the subjonctif. The passé composé a compris becomes ait compris in the subjonctif passé.

cards.de: We went home after he had left.
cards.fr: Nous sommes rentrés après qu'il soit parti.
cards.answer: Nous sommes rentrés après qu'il est parti.
cards.note: après que takes the indicative; only avant que takes the subjonctif. Even native speakers mix these two up.

cards.de: I'm glad you solved the problem.
cards.answer: Je suis heureux que vous ayez résolu le problème.
accept: Je suis content que vous ayez résolu le problème.
Je suis heureuse que vous ayez résolu le problème.
cards.note: Expressions of feeling like être heureux que trigger the subjonctif. Since the action happened earlier, you use the subjonctif passé.

cards.task: Rewrite with «Je ne crois pas que».
cards.answer: Je ne crois pas qu'il ait oublié notre rendez-vous.
cards.note: Negated croire que takes the subjonctif. The passé composé then becomes the subjonctif passé.

cards.answer: Il se peut que vous vous soyez trompés d'adresse.
cards.note: Reflexive verbs always form compound tenses with être, hence vous vous soyez trompés. Il se peut que expresses possibility and takes the subjonctif.

cards.de: That's the best film I've seen this year.
cards.fr: C'est le meilleur film que j'___ vu cette année.
cards.note: After a superlative and after le seul or le premier, the relative clause takes the subjonctif. The je form is j'aie.
The imperative of aller is va, but the -s comes back before y and en: vas-y. It is purely for ease of pronunciation.
Unlike -er verbs, croire keeps its s in the tu form, so crois never loses it. Nous and vous use the croy- stem, exactly as in the present indicative.
Suis! keeps the final s (no -er verb drop) and is the same shape as the être form, but suis-moi can only mean follow me. Nous and vous simply reuse the present forms.
Tu prends keeps its silent ds ending from the present, though you hear only "pran". Prenons and prenez lose the d sound entirely.
These are the present forms with the pronoun simply dropped, so tu keeps its s: viens, never "vien". Watch the vowel shift between viens and venons/venez.

These commands borrow the subjunctive stem sach-, not the present sais/savons, so sache and sachez feel quite different from the indicative. They usually mean be aware rather than know: sache que c'est important.
Vois keeps its s, unlike regular -er commands. The other two are identical to the present indicative forms, and voyons is often just a spoken nudge meaning come on now.
The trap is vous dites, never "disez"; it matches the odd indicative form. Tu dis keeps its s, unlike -er verbs which drop it.
The tu form loses the s of tu vas, so it is va, not vas. The s comes back only before y, as in vas-y.

The tu form keeps its s, unlike parle or va. Watch the pronunciation of the nous form: the ai sounds like the e in petit, and the vous form is one of only three French verbs ending in -tes rather than -ez.
The imperative uses the subjunctive stem, giving aie (no s) and ayons/ayez with y, quite unlike the present as, avons, avez. Mostly heard in fixed advice such as aie confiance and n'ayez pas peur.

The imperative borrows the subjunctive stem soy-, so the tu form is sois with no s-less shortcut, and soyons/soyez keep the y that never appears in the present tense. Very common in set phrases like sois sage and soyez les bienvenus.

cards.fr: Ne dis-moi pas que tu as oublié !
cards.answer: Ne me dis pas que tu as oublié !
cards.note: In a negative imperative the pronoun goes back in front of the verb and is me, not moi.
With reflexive verbs, toi becomes te in the negative imperative and moves before the verb: ne te ... pas.

cards.answer: Aie de la patience et ne t'inquiète pas.
accept: Sois patient et ne t'inquiète pas.
Aie de la patience et ne te fais pas de souci.
cards.note: aie comes from avoir, and -er verbs drop the -s in the tu imperative: inquiète. In the negative, te goes before the verb.
Verbs ending in -er drop the -s in the tu imperative: tu manges, but mange !

cards.de: Tell me if you need help. (speaking to several people)
cards.answer: Dites-le-moi si vous avez besoin d'aide.
accept: Dites-le-moi si vous avez besoin d'aide !
cards.note: With two pronouns in an affirmative imperative, the direct one comes first, then the indirect: dites-le-moi.

cards.fr: Je me suis blessé en ___ du sport.
cards.note: The gérondif is en + the nous stem of the présent + -ant: nous faisons → en faisant.
Voyant keeps the y of nous voyons, and prenant, venant, devant, voulant all come straight from the nous stem. Sachant is the odd one out: it comes from the subjunctive stem, not from nous savons.

Most of these are built on the nous form minus -ons: faisons gives faisant, allons gives allant, disons gives disant, pouvons gives pouvant. Étant and ayant break that pattern, and faisant keeps the ai spelling while sounding like fe-sant.

cards.de: After he had eaten, he left.
cards.note: Après takes a perfect infinitive: après avoir mangé, après être parti. Only possible when both clauses share the same subject.

cards.de: By working a lot, he is making progress.
cards.note: English "by doing something" is normally the gérondif in French. After en you always use the -ant form, never an infinitive.

cards.de: You learn languages by speaking them.
cards.fr: On apprend les langues en les ___.
cards.note: Object pronouns go between en and the gérondif: en les parlant, en me levant.

cards.fr: Après qu'il a fini son travail, il est rentré.
cards.answer: Après avoir fini son travail, il est rentré.
cards.note: When both clauses have the same subject, après avoir + past participle replaces the après que clause.

cards.fr: Quand elle est arrivée à Paris, elle a cherché un appartement.
cards.answer: Après être arrivée à Paris, elle a cherché un appartement.
cards.note: With être verbs the participle agrees with the subject: après être arrivée (she), après être arrivés (we).

cards.de: After I had got up, I took a shower.
cards.fr: Après avoir me levé, j'ai pris une douche.
cards.answer: Après m'être levé, j'ai pris une douche.
accept: Après m'être levée, j'ai pris une douche.
cards.note: Reflexive verbs form the infinitif passé with être, and the reflexive pronoun sits right before it: après m'être levé.

cards.de: He succeeded because he worked a lot.
cards.fr: Il a réussi par travailler beaucoup.
cards.answer: Il a réussi en travaillant beaucoup.
cards.note: Means or manner is expressed by the gérondif. French never uses par + infinitive for this.

cards.de: Before I answer, I think it over.
cards.note: Avant de takes a plain infinitive, while après takes the perfect infinitive: avant de partir, après être parti.

cards.de: After we had arrived, we unpacked the suitcases.
cards.answer: Après être arrivés, nous avons défait les valises.
accept: Après être arrivés, nous avons déballé les valises.
Après être arrivées, nous avons défait les valises.
cards.note: Après is never followed by a conjugated verb, but by être plus a participle that agrees with the subject.

cards.de: After they had gone out, they had a coffee.
cards.fr: Après être ___, elles ont pris un café.
cards.note: The subject elles is feminine plural, so the participle takes the ending -es.

cards.de: He listens to music while he works.
cards.fr: Il écoute de la musique tout ___ travaillant.
cards.note: Tout en plus gérondif stresses simultaneity or a contrast. The en can never be left out.

cards.de: After I had listened to him, I changed my mind.
cards.note: The object pronoun goes before the auxiliary of the infinitif passé: après l'avoir vu, après les avoir appelés.

cards.de: Being ill, she stayed at home.
cards.fr: ___ malade, elle est restée à la maison.
cards.note: To give a reason, use the participe présent without en. The gérondif with en expresses simultaneity, means or condition.
Fut is the passé simple of être. In narrative texts read it as a passé composé. You never need it when speaking.

Voulut, sut, dut and prit are recognisable from the past participles (voulu, su, dû, pris). Careful with il vit (saw) against il vint (came), one letter apart, and il vit is also the present of vivre.

These short third person forms are the ones you meet in novels: fut, eut, fit, put have stems nothing like the infinitive, while alla is regular. The trap is il dit, identical to the present tense, so only the surrounding story tells you which it is.
Fit is the passé simple of faire. It means the same as the passé composé and appears only in written narrative.
Eurent is the passé simple of avoir, third person plural. The forms eus, eut, eurent belong to avoir, not to être.
Devint is the passé simple of devenir and marks a single event in history. The imparfait devenait would describe an ongoing process.
Durent comes from devoir, dirent from dire. The two forms look very similar, so watch the vowel.

cards.de: It was necessary for him to be there.
cards.note: Fût with the accent is subjonctif imparfait, fut without it is passé simple. After il fallait que, literary texts use fût.

cards.de: He saw the light and understood everything.
cards.fr: Il ___ la lumière et comprit tout.
cards.note: vit is the passé simple of voir. The same form is also the present tense of vivre, so the context tells you which one it is.

cards.de: The guests arrived and talked for a long time.
cards.note: -er verbs form the passé simple with -a, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent. The ending -èrent is the easiest one to spot.

cards.de: Then he took the book and read the first page.
cards.fr: Alors il prit le livre et ___ la première page.
cards.note: Many irregular verbs have a u-stem in the passé simple, such as lut from lire, put from pouvoir and sut from savoir.

cards.fr: Ils prirent le train et partirent aussitôt.
cards.answer: Ils ont pris le train et sont partis aussitôt.
accept: Ils ont pris le train et ils sont partis aussitôt.
cards.note: prirent comes from prendre and partirent from partir. In spoken French you would always use the passé composé here.

cards.fr: Elle voulut répondre, mais elle ne put rien dire.
cards.answer: Elle a voulu répondre, mais elle n'a rien pu dire.
accept: Elle a voulu répondre, mais elle n'a pu rien dire.
cards.note: voulut belongs to vouloir and put to pouvoir. In the passé composé, rien slips in between the auxiliary and the participle.

cards.fr: Il naquit à Lyon et mourut à Paris.
cards.answer: Il est né à Lyon et est mort à Paris.
accept: Il est né à Lyon et il est mort à Paris.
cards.note: naquit from naître and mourut from mourir turn up above all in biographies. Both take être in the passé composé.

cards.de: Yesterday he went to the market.
cards.answer: Hier, il est allé au marché.
cards.note: The passé simple belongs in literary or historical writing. Talking about your own day, you use the passé composé.
arriver forms the passé composé with être, so the participle agrees with the subject.
sortir with a direct object takes avoir: j'ai sorti la poubelle. With no object it takes être: je suis sorti. The same goes for monter, descendre, passer and rentrer.

cards.de: We stayed at home on Sunday.
cards.note: rester is one of the verbs of movement and state that take être. The participle agrees with the subject.
nager forms the passé composé with avoir, like most verbs. Only a small, fixed group takes être, even if the verb describes movement.
Reflexive verbs always take être. Here lavé stays unchanged because the direct object les mains comes after the verb.

cards.de: He went down the stairs and opened the door.
cards.fr: Il ___ l'escalier et il a ouvert la porte.
cards.note: descendre takes avoir when it has a direct object, here l'escalier. With no object you say il est descendu.

cards.de: We dropped in on some friends yesterday evening.
cards.answer: Nous sommes passés chez des amis hier soir.
accept: On est passés chez des amis hier soir.
Nous sommes passées chez des amis hier soir.
cards.note: passer in the sense of dropping by takes être. With a direct object it takes avoir: j'ai passé une semaine à Lyon.
monter takes avoir when it has a direct object. With no object you say elle est montée.

cards.de: How long did you run for?
cards.note: courir, marcher and voyager take avoir even though they describe movement. Only the small group such as aller, venir and partir takes être.

cards.de: I went to the cinema yesterday.
cards.answer: Je suis allé au cinéma hier.
accept: Je suis allée au cinéma hier.
cards.note: aller always takes être and never avoir. The participle agrees with the subject.

cards.fr: Elle sort le chien à huit heures.
cards.answer: Elle a sorti le chien à huit heures.
cards.note: sortir with a direct object means to take something out and takes avoir. With no object: elle est sortie à huit heures.

cards.de: The glass fell on the floor.
cards.answer: Le verre est tombé par terre.
accept: Le verre est tombé sur le sol.
cards.note: tomber always takes être and never has an avoir version. The participle agrees with the subject.
