With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object that comes before the verb. Here que stands for les pommes (f pl).
With reflexive verbs there is agreement when se is the direct object. But compare Elle s'est lavé les mains, where the direct object is les mains.
With être verbs the participle always agrees with the subject. Mes sœurs is feminine plural, so arrivées.
sortir forms its passé composé with être, so the participle agrees with the subject Marie: sortie.

cards.de: I met them yesterday. (my female cousins)
cards.note: The pronoun les comes before the verb and is the direct object. It refers to female people in the plural, so rencontrées.
After the pronoun en the participle never agrees. It stays in its basic form.
The direct object is la jambe and it follows the verb. Here se is indirect, so no agreement.

cards.de: The children got up too late.
cards.answer: Les enfants se sont levés trop tard.
accept: Les enfants se sont levés trop tard !
cards.note: With se lever, se is the direct object, so the participle agrees with the subject: levés.

cards.task: Replace the object with a pronoun.
cards.note: The pronoun les moves the direct object in front of the verb, so the participle becomes vues (f pl).

cards.de: The doors were closed at eight o'clock.
cards.fr: Les portes ont été ___ à huit heures.
cards.note: In the passive with être the participle agrees with the subject. Les portes is feminine plural.

cards.de: The two sisters saw each other at the station.
cards.answer: Les deux sœurs se sont vues à la gare.
accept: Les deux sœurs se sont vues à la gare !
cards.note: In reciprocal se voir, se is the direct object, so we get vues. With se parler or se téléphoner the participle stays unchanged.
The passive is être in the same tense plus a participle that agrees with the subject. In everyday French, a sentence with on often sounds more natural.

cards.de: The door was opened by the caretaker.
cards.fr: La porte a été ouverte ___ le concierge.
cards.note: The person doing the action is normally introduced by par. Only verbs of feeling or state take de, as in il est aimé de tous.

cards.de: I was told that the museum was closed.
cards.answer: On m'a dit que le musée était fermé.
accept: On m'a dit que le musée est fermé.
cards.note: An English passive like "I was told" has no direct French equivalent. Use on plus an indirect object pronoun, never j'ai été dit.

cards.de: She was run over by a car.
cards.fr: Elle s'est faite renverser par une voiture.
cards.answer: Elle s'est fait renverser par une voiture.
cards.note: In the construction se faire + infinitive, fait never agrees, because the reflexive pronoun is not the direct object.
For general statements about things, French likes the reflexive passive: ça se mange, ce livre se vend bien.

cards.answer: L'incendie a été éteint par les pompiers.
cards.note: The direct object becomes the subject and the agent follows with par. The tense stays the same, here the passé composé.

cards.fr: Cette langue est parlée au Canada.
cards.answer: On parle cette langue au Canada.
cards.note: When the agent is unknown or unimportant, French often prefers on to a passive.

cards.de: The windows were opened by the wind.
cards.fr: Les fenêtres ont été ouvert par le vent.
cards.answer: Les fenêtres ont été ouvertes par le vent.
cards.note: In the passive the participle always agrees with the subject, so les fenêtres gives ouvertes.

cards.de: The car is being repaired tomorrow.
accept: La voiture va être réparée demain.
cards.note: An English present with future meaning becomes futur simple or futur proche in French. A sentence with on also works here.

cards.de: She's always making fun of my accent.
cards.fr: Elle se moque toujours ___ mon accent.
cards.note: se moquer always takes de, never sur: se moquer de quelqu'un.
In the affirmative imperative the pronouns follow the verb, and te becomes t' before en: va-t'en, allons-nous-en.

cards.fr: Nous nous avons moqués de lui.
cards.answer: Nous nous sommes moqués de lui.
cards.note: All pronominal verbs form the passé composé with être, never with avoir.
In the negative imperative the pronoun stays in front of the verb: ne te moque pas, ne vous moquez pas.
In the passé composé, se and en come before the auxiliary être: je m'en suis allé, ils s'en sont allés.

cards.de: She made fun of me in front of everyone.
cards.fr: Elle s'est moqué de moi devant tout le monde.
cards.answer: Elle s'est moquée de moi devant tout le monde.
cards.note: With se moquer the reflexive pronoun is the direct object, so the participle agrees with the subject. With se rendre compte, rendu stays unchanged.

cards.fr: Il s'en va tout de suite.
cards.task: Make it negative with ne ... pas.
cards.answer: Il ne s'en va pas tout de suite.
cards.note: ne goes before the reflexive pronoun and pas after the conjugated verb: il ne s'en va pas.

cards.de: When I was little, I went to the seaside every summer.
cards.fr: Quand j'étais petit, ___ à la mer chaque été.
cards.note: A repeated habit in the past takes the imparfait. chaque été is the giveaway. Before a vowel je becomes j': j'allais.

Chaque été triggers the imparfait for repetition (allions), while lundi dernier and tout de suite point to one finished event. Note that pleuvait is the background to je lisais, and est arrivé takes être while ont commencé takes avoir.

The imparfait items all describe background or ongoing states (faisait froid, était pleine, dormais), while soudain, à minuit and ce jour-là signal single completed events. Dormais versus ai vu in the same sentence shows the pattern: the frame is imparfait, the interruption is passé composé.

cards.de: I was reading when the phone rang.
cards.note: The ongoing background action goes in the imparfait, the event that cuts into it in the passé composé.

cards.de: The sun was shining and the birds were singing.
cards.fr: Le soleil a brillé et les oiseaux ont chanté.
cards.answer: Le soleil brillait et les oiseaux chantaient.
cards.note: Descriptions of scenery, weather and mood take the imparfait. The passé composé would report them as single finished events.

cards.de: I lived in Lyon for three years.
cards.fr: J'___ à Lyon pendant trois ans.
cards.note: A period with clear limits (pendant trois ans) is finished, so the passé composé is used. The imparfait would suggest an open, unfinished state.

cards.de: I didn't know that she was ill.
cards.fr: Je ne ___ pas qu'elle était malade.
cards.note: This is a state of knowledge, not the moment of finding out. Mental states take the imparfait.

cards.de: I wanted to call you, but I didn't have your number.
cards.answer: Je voulais t'appeler, mais je n'avais pas ton numéro.
accept: Je voulais t'appeler mais je n'avais pas ton numéro.
Je voulais te téléphoner, mais je n'avais pas ton numéro.
cards.note: vouloir and avoir describe an intention and a state here, so the imparfait fits. J'ai voulu t'appeler would mean you actually made the attempt.

cards.fr: Il fait nuit et je marche seul quand une voiture s'arrête devant moi.
cards.task: Put into the past: background in the imparfait, the event in the passé composé.
cards.answer: Il faisait nuit et je marchais seul quand une voiture s'est arrêtée devant moi.
cards.note: The setting (night, walking) continues in the imparfait, while the event that breaks in goes into the passé composé.

cards.de: When he saw the dog, he got frightened.
cards.fr: Quand il a vu le chien, il ___ peur.
cards.note: avoir peur in the passé composé marks the sudden reaction, so it means got scared. Il avait peur would describe a lasting state.
An action with a precise, completed duration needs the passé composé. The imparfait leaves the action open ended.

cards.de: When I arrived, everyone was already there.
cards.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, tout le monde ___ déjà là.
cards.note: The situation you find on arriving is described with the imparfait. Only the arrival itself is an event in the passé composé.

cards.de: While we were eating, he told us the whole story.
cards.answer: Pendant que nous mangions, il nous a raconté toute l'histoire.
accept: Pendant que nous mangions, il nous a raconté toute l'histoire .
cards.note: After pendant que the ongoing action takes the imparfait. The telling is a completed event in the passé composé.

cards.de: If I had known that, I would have come.
cards.fr: Si j'aurais su, je serais venu.
cards.answer: Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
cards.note: For the past: si + plus-que-parfait, main clause in the conditionnel passé. The slip si j'aurais is common, even among native speakers.

The si clause never takes a future or conditional: présent pairs with futur (irai, viendra), imparfait with conditionnel présent (irais, viendrait), plus-que-parfait with conditionnel passé. Both aller and venir take être here, so watch the agreement in serais allé and serait venu.

cards.de: If the weather is nice, we'll eat in the garden.
cards.fr: S'il ___ beau, nous mangerons dans le jardin.
cards.note: Neither the future nor the conditionnel can follow si. The future idea sits only in the main clause: nous mangerons.

cards.fr: Si j'ai le temps, je passerai te voir.
cards.task: Put into the unreal present (si + imparfait).
cards.answer: Si j'avais le temps, je passerais te voir.
cards.note: si + présent/futur becomes si + imparfait plus conditionnel présent. English does the same shift: If I had time, I would drop by.

cards.fr: Si nous partions plus tôt, nous éviterions les bouchons.
cards.answer: Si nous étions partis plus tôt, nous aurions évité les bouchons.
cards.note: The past version is si + plus-que-parfait plus conditionnel passé. Partir forms the plus-que-parfait with être.

cards.de: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
cards.fr: Si je serais riche, j'achèterais une maison.
cards.answer: Si j'étais riche, j'achèterais une maison.
cards.note: After si you need the imparfait; the conditionnel belongs in the main clause. Just as English says if I were, not if I would be.

cards.de: If I were you, I would speak to the boss.
cards.answer: Si j'étais toi, je parlerais au chef.
accept: Si j'étais toi, je parlerais au patron.
Si j'étais à ta place, je parlerais au chef.
À ta place, je parlerais au chef.
cards.note: Si j'étais toi or à ta place are the usual ways to give advice. The verb in the main clause goes in the conditionnel.

cards.de: I don't know if she is coming tomorrow.
cards.fr: Je ne sais pas si elle ___ demain.
cards.note: Here si means whether, not if. In that case the futur and the conditionnel are allowed, unlike in a conditional sentence.

cards.de: If we had arrived earlier, we would have had a seat.
cards.fr: Si nous ___ plus tôt, nous aurions eu de la place.
cards.note: For the unreal past, si takes the plus-que-parfait, here with être. The form serions arrivés is conditionnel passé and only fits the main clause.

cards.de: If you wanted to, we could leave earlier.
cards.fr: Si tu voudrais, on pourrait partir plus tôt.
cards.answer: Si tu voulais, on pourrait partir plus tôt.
accept: Si tu voulais, nous pourrions partir plus tôt.
cards.note: The rule holds for vouloir too: never a conditionnel after si, but the imparfait voulais. The conditionnel pourrait stays in the main clause.

cards.de: If you have time, call me.
cards.fr: Si tu auras le temps, appelle-moi.
cards.answer: Si tu as le temps, appelle-moi.
cards.note: For real conditions, si takes the présent even when you mean the future. The main clause can be an imperative.

cards.de: If you want, we can start tomorrow.
cards.answer: Si tu veux, on peut commencer demain.
accept: Si tu veux, nous pouvons commencer demain.
Si tu veux, on pourra commencer demain.
cards.note: With si + présent the main clause can stay in the présent when the result is certain. Si tu veux is the set phrase for if you like.

cards.de: If we had known that earlier, we would have reacted differently.
cards.answer: Si nous l'avions su plus tôt, nous aurions réagi autrement.
accept: Si on l'avait su plus tôt, on aurait réagi autrement.
Si nous avions su cela plus tôt, nous aurions réagi autrement.
cards.note: Type three: si + plus-que-parfait in the si clause, conditionnel passé in the main clause. English that becomes the pronoun le, placed before the auxiliary.

cards.fr: Si tu ne m'aides pas, je n'y arriverai pas.
cards.task: Put into the unreal present (si + imparfait).
cards.answer: Si tu ne m'aidais pas, je n'y arriverais pas.
cards.note: si + présent becomes si + imparfait, and the futur becomes the conditionnel présent. The negation ne ... pas still wraps around the verb.

cards.de: Even if I had time, I wouldn't come.
cards.fr: Même si j'___ le temps, je ne viendrais pas.
cards.note: Même si follows the same rules as plain si. For the unreal present that means the imparfait, with the conditionnel only in the main clause.

cards.de: Although it's raining, we're going out.
cards.note: bien que, quoique, pour que, avant que, à moins que + subjonctif.

Doubt, necessity and concession trigger the subjonctif (il faut que, bien que, je doute que), while penser que, espérer que and il est certain que in the affirmative keep the indicatif. Watch that espérer que does not take the subjonctif even though it feels uncertain in English.
espérer que takes the indicative, often the futur: j'espère que tu viendras. souhaiter que is different: it takes the subjonctif.
après que takes the indicative; only avant que triggers the subjonctif. Many French speakers still say soit parti, but the indicative is the correct form.
Affirmative je pense que and je crois que state an opinion and take the indicative. Only the negative or a question brings in the subjonctif.

cards.fr: Je ne crois pas qu'il ___ malade.
cards.note: Negated verbs of opinion like ne pas croire and ne pas penser express doubt, so the subjonctif follows.

cards.de: It's a shame you can't come with us.
cards.answer: C'est dommage que tu ne puisses pas venir avec nous.
accept: Dommage que tu ne puisses pas venir avec nous.
C'est dommage que tu ne puisses pas venir.
C'est dommage que tu ne puisses pas nous accompagner.
cards.note: Expressions of feeling such as c'est dommage que, je suis content que, j'ai peur que take the subjonctif. pouvoir gives que je puisse, que tu puisses.

cards.fr: Il est certain qu'elle vient avec nous.
cards.task: Rewrite with « Il n'est pas certain que ».
cards.answer: Il n'est pas certain qu'elle vienne avec nous.
cards.note: Certainty takes the indicative, uncertainty the subjonctif. That is why il est possible que and il n'est pas sûr que call for vienne.

cards.fr: Je voudrais que je parte plus tôt.
cards.note: When both verbs share the same subject, French uses the infinitive instead of que + subjonctif. With two subjects: Je voudrais que tu partes plus tôt.

cards.de: If I have time, I'll come along.
cards.fr: Si j'___ le temps, je viendrai.
cards.note: After si (condition) French uses the present, never the futur. Only quand, lorsque and dès que take the futur.

cards.de: When you come tomorrow, we'll talk about it.
cards.fr: Quand tu viens demain, on en parlera.
cards.answer: Quand tu viendras demain, on en parlera.
cards.note: With a clear future reference (demain), quand must be followed by the futur. Using the present is the typical English speaker's mistake.

cards.de: I'll tell you when I know.
cards.answer: Je te le dirai quand je le saurai.
accept: Je te le dirai dès que je le saurai.
cards.note: Both verbs go in the futur because both events lie in the future. English keeps the present in the when clause.
When you move the sentence into the future, both verbs go into the futur simple, including the one in the quand clause.

cards.de: When I have my diploma, I'll look for a job.
cards.fr: Quand j'___ mon diplôme, je chercherai un travail.
cards.note: When one action is finished before the other, French uses the futur antérieur. The passé composé doesn't work here because everything lies in the future.

cards.de: When it rains, I always take the bus.
cards.fr: Quand il ___, je prends toujours le bus.
cards.note: For habits, quand means "whenever" and takes the présent. The futur only appears when you really are talking about the future.

cards.de: As soon as I've arrived, I'll write to you.
cards.answer: Dès que je serai arrivé, je t'écrirai.
accept: Dès que je serai arrivée, je t'écrirai.
Quand je serai arrivé, je t'écrirai.
cards.note: Where English uses the present perfect after "as soon as", French uses the futur antérieur, because the arriving is finished before the writing.

cards.de: When we have time, we'll visit the museum.
cards.fr: Quand nous ___ le temps, nous visiterons le musée.
cards.note: Avoir and être also go into the futur after quand: j'aurai, je serai, nous aurons.

cards.de: When the weather is nice, we'll go to the beach.
cards.fr: Quand il fera beau, nous ___ à la plage.
cards.note: If the quand clause is in the futur, the main clause normally uses the futur too. The conditionnel would be wrong here.

cards.fr: Il a dit : « Je viendrai demain. »
cards.task: Put into reported speech: Il a dit que …
cards.answer: Il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain.
accept: Il a dit qu'il viendrait demain.
cards.note: With a reporting verb in the past, the futur becomes the conditionnel. Demain becomes le lendemain once that day has gone by.

cards.fr: Elle a dit : « Je suis fatiguée. »
cards.task: Put into reported speech: Elle a dit que …
cards.answer: Elle a dit qu'elle était fatiguée.
cards.note: When the reporting verb is in the past, the présent of the direct speech shifts to the imparfait. The pronoun also changes from je to elle.

cards.fr: Il m'a demandé : « Tu as fini ton travail ? »
cards.task: Put into reported speech: Il m'a demandé …
cards.answer: Il m'a demandé si j'avais fini mon travail.
cards.note: Yes/no questions are introduced by si, not by que. The passé composé shifts to the plus-que-parfait.

cards.de: She told us she had lost her wallet.
cards.fr: Elle a raconté qu'elle ___ son portefeuille.
cards.note: After a reporting verb in the past, the passé composé becomes the plus-que-parfait.

cards.de: He promised that he would be finished before midday.
cards.fr: Il a promis qu'il ___ avant midi.
cards.note: The futur antérieur of direct speech becomes the conditionnel passé when reported. It shows an action completed before a later point.

cards.de: The doctor told him to rest.
cards.fr: Le médecin lui a dit qu'il se repose.
cards.answer: Le médecin lui a dit de se reposer.
accept: Le médecin lui a dit qu'il devait se reposer.
cards.note: A reported order uses de + infinitive in French, much like the English "told him to rest". A que clause does not work here.

cards.de: I don't know where he is.
cards.fr: Je ne sais pas où est-il.
cards.answer: Je ne sais pas où il est.
cards.note: Indirect questions have no inversion. After où, quand or pourquoi you keep the normal order subject + verb.

cards.de: She asked what I would do at the weekend.
cards.answer: Elle a demandé ce que je ferais le week-end.
accept: Elle m'a demandé ce que je ferais le week-end.
cards.note: The question word que becomes ce que in reported speech. The futur of the direct question becomes the conditionnel présent.

cards.de: She asked me whether I wanted a coffee.
cards.fr: Elle m'a demandé ___ je voulais un café.
cards.note: English "whether/if" in a reported question is si. Que follows statement verbs like dire, and ce que is only for asking about a thing.

cards.de: He says that he's coming tomorrow.
accept: Il dit qu'il va venir demain.
cards.note: If the reporting verb is in the présent, no tenses shift. The futur stays futur and demain stays demain.

cards.de: He said that he was ill and that he wouldn't come.
cards.fr: Il a dit qu'il était malade et ___ ne viendrait pas.
cards.note: Que has to be repeated before each further clause. English can drop the second "that", French cannot.

cards.fr: Elle a dit : « Aujourd'hui, je reste à la maison. »
cards.task: Put into reported speech: Elle a dit que …
cards.answer: Elle a dit que ce jour-là elle restait à la maison.
accept: Elle a dit que ce jour-là, elle restait à la maison.
cards.note: Time expressions shift too: aujourd'hui becomes ce jour-là, hier becomes la veille, maintenant becomes à ce moment-là.

cards.de: How long have you been living here?
accept: Depuis quand est-ce que tu habites ici ?
cards.note: French uses depuis with the présent for something still going on, where English needs "have been living".

cards.task: depuis, il y a, pendant or pour?
cards.note: Depuis covers a situation that is still true now, while il y a points back to a finished moment and pendant to a closed stretch of time. Pour looks forward to a planned duration, which is why the booked trip takes pour and not pendant.

cards.de: I met him three years ago.
cards.note: il y a + a length of time means "ago", looking back to a finished point. depuis means "since/for" and the situation still continues.

cards.de: We've been waiting for half an hour.
cards.note: An action that is still going on takes depuis plus the présent in French, even though English uses a perfect form.

cards.de: I worked for two hours last night.
cards.fr: Hier soir, j'ai travaillé ___ deux heures.
cards.note: pendant gives the completed duration of a finished action, usually with the passé composé.

cards.de: I have been learning French for three years.
cards.fr: J'ai appris le français depuis trois ans.
cards.answer: J'apprends le français depuis trois ans.
cards.note: For an action that is still going on, depuis takes the present tense in French, where English uses "have been doing".

cards.de: I haven't seen her since Christmas.
cards.fr: Je ne l'ai pas vue ___ Noël.
cards.note: In negative sentences depuis is followed by the passé composé, because nothing has actually happened.

cards.answer: Il est parti il y a dix minutes.
accept: Il est parti il y a 10 minutes.
cards.note: il y a plus a time expression means "ago" and always goes with a past tense.

cards.de: I have been living in this town for five years.
cards.fr: ___ cinq ans que j'habite dans cette ville.
cards.note: ça fait ... que or il y a ... que at the start of the sentence means the same as depuis. The verb stays in the present.

cards.fr: Ça fait deux mois qu'elle cherche un appartement.
cards.answer: Elle cherche un appartement depuis deux mois.
accept: Elle cherche depuis deux mois un appartement.
cards.note: ça fait ... que and depuis express exactly the same idea. With depuis the normal word order is kept.

cards.de: While I was cooking, he was reading the newspaper.
cards.fr: ___ je cuisinais, il lisait le journal.
cards.note: Before a noun you use pendant; before a full clause with its own verb you need pendant que.

cards.de: I'm going to Spain for three weeks.
cards.fr: Je pars en Espagne ___ trois semaines.
cards.note: For a planned length of time in the future, French uses pour. depuis and il y a do not work here.

cards.de: She had been working at the company for two years when she was promoted.
cards.fr: Elle travaillait dans l'entreprise ___ deux ans quand elle a été promue.
cards.note: When the point of reference lies in the past, depuis is used with the imparfait instead of the present.

cards.fr: Nous sommes arrivés depuis une semaine.
cards.answer: Nous sommes arrivés il y a une semaine.
cards.note: Arriving is a one-off event, so you need il y a. depuis would describe something still going on.

cards.de: During the holidays we read a lot.
cards.answer: Pendant les vacances, nous avons beaucoup lu.
accept: Nous avons beaucoup lu pendant les vacances.
Durant les vacances, nous avons beaucoup lu.
cards.note: pendant plus a noun means "during". The noun normally keeps its article: pendant les vacances.
faire + infinitive means to have something done by someone else. laisser + infinitive means to let something happen: Laisse-moi partir.
faire + infinitive says that something causes or brings about an action. faire rire, faire pleurer and faire attendre never take a preposition.
laisser + infinitive means to let or allow. In the affirmative imperative the pronoun comes after the verb, joined by a hyphen.
The object pronoun goes in front of laisser, not in front of the infinitive. le only becomes l' before a vowel, and here it stands before laisse.
With faire or laisser + infinitive the pronoun attaches to the conjugated verb: je le fais réparer, not je fais le réparer.
Before an infinitive, fait stays invariable even when a direct object pronoun comes first. So never faits or faites.

cards.answer: Je me suis fait couper les cheveux.
cards.note: se faire + infinitive means having something done to yourself. The participle fait always stays invariable in this structure.

cards.de: When you're tired, you can easily drop something.
cards.fr: Quand on est fatigué, on peut facilement ___.
cards.note: laisser tomber literally means to let something fall. Figuratively it means to give up or to let someone down.

cards.de: The teacher has the pupils write a text.
cards.fr: Le professeur fait écrire un texte ___ ses élèves.
cards.note: When the infinitive already has a direct object, the person doing the action is introduced by à or par. With no second object you simply say il fait écrire ses élèves.
To make someone wait is faire attendre, because you cause it. In the negative imperative the pronoun goes back in front of the verb.
This is about allowing, so laisser + infinitive. faire would mean you are making me work.

cards.task: Rewrite with faire + infinitive so it means: I am having my bike repaired.
cards.note: faire + infinitive shows that someone else carries out the action. The object comes straight after the infinitive.
Conditionnel passé of devoir: j'aurais dû + infinitive. Note that French puts the modal idea first, where English says should have come.

cards.de: He must have missed the train.
cards.note: il a dû = he must have (a guess) or he had to. il devait = he was supposed to, a plan that may not have worked out.
Conditionnel passé of pouvoir: j'aurais pu + infinitive. The object pronoun goes before the infinitive, not before aurais.

cards.de: I couldn't come, I had too much work.
cards.fr: Je ___ venir, j'avais trop de travail.
cards.note: A one-off event in the past takes the passé composé: je n'ai pas pu. The imparfait je ne pouvais pas describes an ongoing state or a lasting inability.
The past participle of devoir is dû with a circumflex, not devu.

cards.task: Make it more polite by putting it into the conditionnel présent.
cards.note: Tu dois is a blunt order, tu devrais sounds like advice. The conditionnel softens the statement.

cards.de: She shouldn't have read the letter.
cards.answer: Elle n'aurait pas dû lire la lettre.
cards.note: French has no separate verb for being allowed to in this sense. Not being allowed to is expressed with ne pas devoir.

cards.de: I wanted to call you, but I forgot.
cards.note: An intention in the background takes the imparfait: je voulais. J'ai voulu stresses a completed act of will, more like I really wanted to or I tried to.

cards.fr: Elle a dû de partir tôt.
cards.note: After devoir, pouvoir, vouloir and savoir the infinitive follows directly, with no de or à.
Learned skills take savoir. Il peut nager means he is allowed to or it is possible for him right now.

cards.de: I am waiting for the bus at the stop.
cards.fr: J'attends sur le bus à l'arrêt.
cards.note: attendre takes a direct object with no preposition. The for of English wait for easily tempts you into adding one.
Profiter de, dépendre de and avoir besoin de all take de, while participer à and s'intéresser à take à. Regarder needs nothing, so no à or de creeps in after it.
Commencer à, réussir à and obéir à contrast with décider de and essayer de before an infinitive. Écouter is the odd one out with no preposition at all, unlike English "listen to".
Attendre and chercher take no preposition in French even though English has "wait for" and "look for". Compare penser à quelqu'un with rêver de and se souvenir de.

cards.de: I have been looking for my keys for ten minutes.
cards.fr: Je cherche après mes clés depuis dix minutes.
cards.answer: Je cherche mes clés depuis dix minutes.
cards.note: chercher qc takes a direct object. Do not carry over the for of English look for.

cards.de: I like going to the cinema at the weekend.
cards.note: After aimer, adorer, détester, vouloir, pouvoir, devoir and espérer the infinitive follows with no preposition.

cards.fr: Elle pense à ses prochaines vacances.
cards.task: Replace « à ses prochaines vacances » with a pronoun.
cards.note: With things, a phrase introduced by à is replaced by y, and one introduced by de by en: Elle en parle.

cards.de: Recently my brother has begun to take an interest in politics.
cards.fr: Depuis peu, mon frère commence à ___.
cards.note: The verb takes à: s'intéresser à qc. The noun l'intérêt takes pour instead: l'intérêt pour la politique.

cards.de: Do not forget to call me tomorrow.
accept: N'oublie pas de me téléphoner demain.
cards.note: oublier de faire qc. Before a noun there is no de: J'ai oublié mon parapluie.
demander à qn de faire qc, which is why it is lui (= à lui), not le. The same goes for conseiller, permettre, interdire and dire à qn de faire qc.

cards.task: Fill both gaps: à or de?
cards.note: Demander, dire, conseiller, permettre and proposer all mark the person with à and the action with de: à mon frère de m'aider. The trap is putting de before the person, especially when the person comes first in the sentence.

cards.de: The doctor advised him to stop smoking.
cards.fr: Le médecin ___ a conseillé d'arrêter de fumer.
cards.note: conseiller à qn de faire qc. The person is introduced by à, so the pronoun is lui or leur, never le or la.

cards.de: My parents do not allow me to travel alone.
cards.fr: Mes parents ne me permettent pas ___ voyager seule.
cards.note: permettre à qn de faire qc. de always comes before the infinitive, including in negative sentences.

cards.de: I asked my sister to help me.
cards.fr: J'ai demandé ma sœur de m'aider.
cards.answer: J'ai demandé à ma sœur de m'aider.
cards.note: The pattern is demander à qn de faire qc. In French the person is an indirect object, unlike English ask someone.

cards.de: The teacher has forbidden us to use the mobile phone.
cards.answer: Le professeur nous a interdit d'utiliser le portable.
accept: Le prof nous a interdit d'utiliser le portable.
Le professeur nous a interdit d'utiliser le téléphone portable.
cards.note: interdire à qn de faire qc. With nous and vous you cannot see whether the object is direct or indirect, but the pattern is the same.

cards.de: In French you always say: to advise someone to do something.
cards.answer: conseiller à qn de faire qc
accept: conseiller à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose
cards.note: Learn it as a formula: conseiller à qn de faire qc. demander, permettre, interdire, promettre, proposer and dire all work the same way.

cards.de: He promised them to be on time.
cards.fr: Il ___ a promis d'être à l'heure.
cards.note: promettre à qn de faire qc. The plural of lui is leur, with no s, and it goes before the verb.

cards.de: She suggested to me that we go to the cinema.
cards.note: proposer à qn de faire qc. The participle stays unchanged because m' is an indirect object here.

cards.fr: Dis à tes amis qu'ils doivent venir plus tôt.
cards.task: Rephrase using dire à qn de faire qc.
cards.answer: Dis à tes amis de venir plus tôt.
cards.note: Instead of a que clause, dire à qn is normally followed by de + infinitive when you are telling someone to do something.

cards.de: My father forbids her to go out.
cards.answer: Mon père lui interdit de sortir.
cards.note: interdire takes à qn, so you need lui, not l'. What is forbidden is the action, not the person.

cards.de: I advised her not to go.
cards.fr: Je lui ai conseillé de ___ partir.
cards.note: With an infinitive, ne and pas stay together in front of the verb: de ne pas partir.

cards.de: Will you let me take your car?
cards.answer: Tu me permets de prendre ta voiture ?
accept: Est-ce que tu me permets de prendre ta voiture ?
Me permets-tu de prendre ta voiture ?
cards.note: permettre à qn de faire qc. The pronoun me comes before the conjugated verb, and de before the infinitive.

cards.de: I asked him if he was coming.
cards.note: de + infinitive is only used when you are asking someone to do something. In an indirect question you need si plus a full clause. Before il and ils, si becomes s': s'il venait.

cards.de: I am waiting for the bus.
cards.note: Trap: attendre takes a direct object, so there is no word for the English for. The same happens with chercher (look for) and payer (pay for).
English phones someone directly, but French needs téléphoner à qn. With a pronoun: je lui téléphone. Same pattern with obéir à qn and ressembler à qn.

cards.de: We have been waiting for you for an hour.
cards.note: Two traps: attendre needs no preposition, and French uses the present tense with depuis where English uses have been waiting. The object is direct, so te, le, la, les, never lui.

cards.de: I am looking for my passport.
cards.note: chercher already means look for, so adding pour or après is wrong in standard French.
English obeys someone directly, but French always needs obéir à qn. With a pronoun: il lui obéit.
écouter qn takes a direct object, so there is no à and no to. Use me, le, la, les (m'écouter, l'écouter), never lui. Same with regarder qn.

cards.fr: Il a payé pour les billets.
cards.note: payer qc has no preposition. Use pour only for the person you pay on behalf of: j'ai payé pour mon frère.

cards.answer: Elle se marie avec un Italien.
cards.note: English marries someone directly, but se marier needs avec. Only épouser qn works without a preposition.
se marier is always followed by avec. The English direct object becomes a prepositional phrase in French.

cards.de: In French you say wait for someone without a preposition.
cards.fr: En français, on dit ___ sans préposition.
cards.note: The English for in wait for has no equivalent in French. The same is true of chercher qc (look for) and payer qc (pay for).

cards.de: I am calling them (my parents) this evening.
cards.note: téléphoner à qn has an indirect object, so it is lui in the singular and leur in the plural, never les, even though English says call them.

cards.task: Replace the object with a pronoun.
cards.note: regarder qn means look at someone but takes a direct object, so the pronoun is le, la or les, never lui or leur.

cards.fr: Je cherche mes lunettes depuis ce matin.
cards.task: Replace the object with a pronoun.
cards.answer: Je les cherche depuis ce matin.
cards.note: chercher qc is direct, so the pronoun is les, not leur or en, even though English says looking for them.
Thing + facile à faire: C'est facile à comprendre. With impersonal il and an object after the infinitive: Il est facile de comprendre ça.
Sûr, obligé, heureux and plein all pair with de, so prêt à partir is the one that breaks the run. Utile takes à when you name the person it helps: utile à tous les voyageurs.

Content, capable and fier take de; prêt and habitué take à. Difficile à comprendre uses à because the thing understood (ce texte) is already the subject; with a dummy il it would be il est difficile de comprendre.

cards.de: I am ready to help you.
cards.note: prêt is always followed by à + infinitive. Learn prêt à as a fixed pair.

cards.de: He is not able to work on his own.
cards.fr: Il n'est pas capable ___ travailler seul.
cards.note: capable takes de + infinitive. Remember the contrasting pair: prêt à, but capable de.

cards.fr: Il est facile de trouver cet hôtel.
cards.task: Rephrase without the impersonal il, using cet hôtel as the subject.
cards.answer: Cet hôtel est facile à trouver.
cards.note: When a thing is the subject, you get facile à + infinitive with no object after it. The impersonal version is il est facile de + infinitive plus an object.

cards.de: It is difficult to get up early.
cards.fr: Il est difficile à se lever tôt.
cards.answer: Il est difficile de se lever tôt.
cards.note: After impersonal il est + adjective you need de + infinitive. The à only belongs in sentences like ce texte est difficile à lire.

cards.de: This word is easy to remember.
cards.fr: Ce mot est facile de retenir.
cards.answer: Ce mot est facile à retenir.
cards.note: When the subject is a concrete thing that you remember, read or do, the pattern is thing + facile à + infinitive.

cards.de: She is proud of her daughter.
cards.answer: Elle est fière de sa fille.
accept: Elle est fière de sa fille !
cards.note: fier de happens to match English "proud of", but French prepositions often differ from ours, so learn each adjective together with its preposition.

cards.de: To win, you have to be ready for anything.
cards.note: prêt à is used not only before an infinitive but also before a noun or pronoun such as tout. The adjective agrees with the person: elle est prête.

cards.de: We are glad to see you.
cards.note: Adjectives of feeling such as content, heureux, triste and fier take de + infinitive.

cards.de: This handwriting is impossible to read.
cards.note: Like facile and difficile, impossible follows the pattern thing + à + infinitive. Impersonally: il est impossible de lire cette écriture.

cards.de: I am not used to getting up so early.
cards.fr: Je ne suis pas habitué ___ me lever si tôt.
cards.note: habitué belongs to the à group, along with prêt à, décidé à and occupé à.

cards.de: It is impossible to reach him today.
cards.answer: Il est impossible de le joindre aujourd'hui.
accept: Il est impossible de le contacter aujourd'hui.
C'est impossible de le joindre aujourd'hui.
cards.note: When an object follows the infinitive, use the impersonal form il est impossible de. The c'est version is common in speech.

cards.de: a coffee cup (the cup made for coffee)
cards.note: à marks purpose: une tasse à café is the cup itself. de marks contents: une tasse de café is a cup of coffee.
Raison, envie, droit and peur all take de, and de is also what comes before an infinitive after a noun. Réponse and solution are the exceptions with à, pointing to what is being answered or solved.

cards.de: I'm drinking a glass of wine.
cards.note: de gives the contents: un verre de vin is a glass with wine in it. With à it would be the empty wine glass.

cards.de: He's taking his backpack with him.
cards.fr: Il emporte son sac de dos.
cards.answer: Il emporte son sac à dos.
cards.note: Purpose takes à: un sac à dos, un sac à main. With de you would be naming the contents.

cards.de: Can you pass me the iron (for clothes)?
cards.fr: Tu peux me passer le fer ___ repasser ?
cards.note: Before an infinitive after a noun, French uses à, not pour or de: un fer à repasser, une planche à repasser.

cards.de: She's eating a plate of soup.
cards.fr: Elle mange une assiette à soupe.
cards.answer: Elle mange une assiette de soupe.
cards.note: What you eat is the contents, so de. Une assiette à soupe would be the soup bowl itself.

cards.de: Have you packed your swimming costume?
cards.fr: Tu as pris ton maillot ___ bain ?
cards.note: A few set phrases take de even though they express purpose: un maillot de bain, une salle de bains, une serviette de bain.

cards.de: I'd like a bottle of water and two teacups.
cards.answer: Je voudrais une bouteille d'eau et deux tasses à thé.
accept: J'aimerais une bouteille d'eau et deux tasses à thé.
Je voudrais une bouteille d'eau et deux tasses à thé, s'il vous plaît.
cards.note: Both appear in one sentence: de for what is in the bottle, à for what the cups are for. Before a vowel, de becomes d'.
City names always take à, never en: à Lyon, à Berlin, à Rome.
Plural countries take aux, and cities take bare à with no article. Iran is masculine but still takes en because it begins with a vowel, so au Iran is wrong.
The three feminine countries take en, the three masculine ones take au. Note that en absorbs the article completely, so there is no en la France.

cards.de: I'm going to the doctor today.
cards.answer: Je vais chez le médecin aujourd'hui.
cards.note: Use chez before people: chez le médecin, chez le coiffeur, chez Paul. à or au is only for places.

cards.de: These flowers come from the Netherlands.
cards.note: With plural country names, de + les contracts to des: venir des Pays-Bas, revenir des États-Unis.

cards.task: Replace the country with le Canada.
cards.note: With masculine countries starting with a consonant, à + le becomes au: au Canada, au Japon, au Maroc.

cards.de: We're going to Paris in July.
cards.fr: Nous allons en Paris en juillet.
cards.answer: Nous allons à Paris en juillet.
cards.note: en is only used with countries and regions; cities always take à. English to is à here.

cards.de: I go to work by bike.
cards.note: Use à when you sit on it or move under your own power: à vélo, à pied, à cheval. Use en for vehicles you sit inside: en voiture, en train. You will also hear en vélo informally.
En is used when you get inside the vehicle (voiture, avion, train), à when you sit on it or use your own body (pied, vélo, cheval). À pied is the one learners often turn into en pied.

cards.de: On the train I read my book.
cards.fr: ___ le train, j'ai lu mon livre.
cards.note: When you mean the inside of the vehicle as a place, use dans le train, dans le bus, dans la voiture. En train only describes the means of travel.

cards.de: I go into town by bus.
cards.fr: Je vais en ville avec le bus.
cards.answer: Je vais en ville en bus.
accept: Je vais en ville en autobus.
cards.note: By bus is en bus, not avec le bus. French uses avec only for people or things you take along with you.
en avion is the everyday form. par avion appears mainly on post and in formal writing.

cards.de: We're going on an excursion on horseback.
cards.note: When you sit on the vehicle or animal rather than inside it, use à: à cheval, à vélo, à moto.

cards.de: I take the metro every morning.
cards.answer: Je prends le métro chaque matin.
accept: Je prends le métro tous les matins.
Chaque matin, je prends le métro.
cards.note: With prendre, the means of transport keeps its article: prendre le métro, prendre le train, prendre la voiture.

cards.de: On my bike I always wear a helmet.
cards.fr: À le vélo, je porte toujours un casque.
cards.answer: À vélo, je porte toujours un casque.
accept: Sur mon vélo, je porte toujours un casque.
cards.note: After à the means of transport takes no article, so à vélo. With an article you need a different preposition: sur le vélo.
en taxi describes the way you travel and takes no article. Dans le taxi would mean inside the car.

cards.de: I'll be back in two hours.
cards.note: dans = after two hours have passed (a point in the future). en = within that stretch of time (how long something takes): J'ai fait ça en deux heures.
En for how long something takes, dans for when it will start, pendant for a stretch, à for a clock time.

cards.de: The train leaves in five minutes.
cards.note: dans points to a moment in the future, once the five minutes are up. en would suggest that the departure itself takes five minutes.
For a duration that has actually elapsed, French uses pendant, never pour, even though English says "for". pendant can often be dropped altogether.

cards.de: I'm going to Canada for a year.
cards.fr: Je pars au Canada ___ un an.
cards.note: pour gives a planned or intended length of stay in the future, usually after verbs like partir, venir or rester.

cards.de: She's arriving in half an hour.
cards.note: This is a point in the future, so dans. en une demi-heure would mean the arriving itself takes half an hour.

cards.de: He wrote the letter in five minutes.
cards.answer: Il a écrit la lettre en cinq minutes.
accept: Il a rédigé la lettre en cinq minutes.
cards.note: Here what counts is the time needed for a completed action, so en. English "in" can be either en or dans.

cards.fr: Je finirai ce travail dans une heure.
cards.task: Rewrite it so that the work itself takes an hour.
cards.answer: Je finirai ce travail en une heure.
cards.note: dans une heure means an hour from now, en une heure means within one hour of working.
pendant gives the period within which something happens. Pour would be wrong here, since it only marks a planned duration.

cards.de: She went to London for three days.
cards.answer: Elle est partie à Londres pour trois jours.
accept: Elle est allée à Londres pour trois jours.
cards.note: English "for" with a planned length of stay corresponds to pour. For a duration already completed you would use pendant.

cards.de: I live in the Rue Victor Hugo.
cards.note: It is dans la rue, but sur le boulevard, sur l'avenue, sur la place.

Devant and derrière refer to front and back, not above and below, so do not let sur and sous pull them in. Contre means touching the wall while entre needs two reference points, here the sofa and the window.

cards.de: In the photo you can see my grandmother.
cards.fr: ___ la photo, on voit ma grand-mère.
cards.note: With pictures, photos and maps French uses sur, where English says "in": sur la photo, sur le tableau, sur la carte.

cards.de: There are a lot of people in the street.
cards.answer: Il y a beaucoup de monde dans la rue.
accept: Il y a beaucoup de gens dans la rue.
cards.note: French says dans la rue, because the street is pictured as a space between the buildings. Never sur la rue.

cards.de: I read that in the newspaper.
cards.fr: J'ai lu ça sur le journal.
cards.answer: J'ai lu ça dans le journal.
cards.note: Texts take dans: dans le journal, dans le livre, dans un mail. Only for websites do you say sur.

cards.de: There's a film on television tonight.
cards.fr: Il y a un film ___ télé ce soir.
cards.note: Media take à: à la télé, à la radio, au cinéma. Dans la télé would mean physically inside the set.

cards.de: I slept the whole time on the train.
cards.fr: J'ai dormi tout le temps ___ le train.
cards.note: Vehicles you get inside take dans, even where English says on: dans le train, dans le bus, dans l'avion.

cards.de: The market is on the square in front of the church.
cards.answer: Le marché est sur la place devant l'église.
accept: Le marché se trouve sur la place devant l'église.
cards.note: Open spaces take sur: sur la place, sur le parking, sur le trottoir.

cards.de: You can find the village easily on the map.
cards.fr: Tu trouves facilement le village dans la carte.
cards.answer: Tu trouves facilement le village sur la carte.
cards.note: Flat surfaces showing an image take sur: sur la carte, sur le plan, sur l'écran.

cards.de: I don't go there any more.
cards.note: y stands for there. Pronouns go directly before the verb, inside ne … plus.

En says how long something took to finish, dans when it starts, and pendant how long it lasted. Depuis needs an action still going on, and vers gives an approximate clock time where à gives an exact one.
ne … que means only. que goes immediately before the word it limits.

cards.de: I didn't find a single mistake.
cards.note: aucun/aucune is always singular and takes no article. It replaces pas de and stresses not a single one.

cards.fr: Il fait plus froid que je ___ pensais.
cards.note: After a comparison with plus/moins … que, French often adds a ne explétif. It negates nothing and has no English equivalent.

cards.de: I'm afraid he'll arrive too late.
cards.note: craindre, avoir peur and avant que often take a ne explétif with the subjonctif. Only adding pas makes it a real negation.
Even when personne, rien or aucun is the subject, ne still has to stand before the verb.
rien can be the subject, and then it needs ne before the verb. pas is never added.

cards.answer: Je n'ai jamais vu ce film.
cards.note: déjà becomes ne … jamais in the negative. In the passé composé, jamais sits between the auxiliary and the participle.

cards.de: I'll never make this mistake again.
cards.note: plus and jamais can be combined, always in that order. Both follow the conjugated verb: Je ne le ferai plus jamais.

cards.de: I hope I haven't made a mistake.
cards.note: With a negated infinitive, ne pas stays together in front of the auxiliary avoir or être.

cards.answer: Il est parti sans rien dire.
accept: Il est parti sans rien dire du tout.
cards.note: No ne is used after sans. Rien and personne come before the infinitive: sans voir personne.

cards.task: Turn into a question using inversion.
cards.note: Inversion: verb, hyphen, pronoun. It sounds formal. With est-ce que: Est-ce que tu as faim ?
Qu'est-ce qui asks about the subject (what happened?). Qu'est-ce que asks about the object (what are you doing?).
In short questions with où, quand or comment, the verb can come straight before the noun. Also possible: Où est-ce que ta sœur habite ?

cards.de: What are you doing at the weekend?
cards.fr: Qu'est-ce qui tu fais le week-end ?
cards.answer: Qu'est-ce que tu fais le week-end ?
cards.note: Qu'est-ce qui is followed by a verb, qu'est-ce que by a subject. Here tu follows, so it must be qu'est-ce que.
If the verb form ends in a vowel, a t is inserted before il, elle or on. That gives arrive-t-il, a-t-elle, parle-t-on.
After a preposition, use qui for people and quoi for things. Que can never follow a preposition.

accept: De quoi est-ce que vous parlez ?
cards.note: English puts the preposition at the end, but French puts it first: preposition plus quoi. The verb parler takes de.

accept: Est-ce que ton frère vient aussi ?
cards.note: A noun subject is not moved behind the verb in inversion. It stays in front and is echoed by a pronoun.
The first part shows whether you mean a person or a thing, the second whether you are asking about the subject or the object. The short Qui t'a appelé ? works too.

cards.task: Rewrite as a question with inversion.
cards.note: With inversion, est-ce que disappears and the subject pronoun moves behind the verb with a hyphen. This form sounds a bit more formal.

cards.de: I don't know what he wants.
cards.note: Indirect questions never use est-ce que. What becomes ce que for the object and ce qui for the subject.
When what is followed by a noun with être, French uses quel, agreeing in number and gender. Quelle est ton idée ? Quels sont tes projets ?
In casual speech the question word often goes at the end. The neutral pattern is question word plus est-ce que plus subject plus verb.
Short que always requires inversion. Without inversion you need qu'est-ce que, or put quoi at the end.

cards.de: I'm the one who did that (not him).
cards.note: C'est … qui highlights the subject. The verb agrees with moi: c'est moi qui ai, c'est nous qui sommes.

cards.de: You're the one who is always late.
cards.fr: C'est toi qui ___ toujours en retard.
cards.note: After c'est toi qui, the verb goes in the second person singular. Qui carries the person of the highlighted pronoun.

cards.de: What I love is the silence.
cards.note: Use ce que when the highlighted element is the object of the verb: j'aime quelque chose. Ce qui is only for the subject.

cards.de: What bothers me is the noise.
cards.fr: Ce ___ me dérange, c'est le bruit.
cards.note: Here the highlighted element is the subject of déranger, so you need ce qui. The second half always starts with c'est.

cards.de: What I need is a holiday.
cards.fr: Ce ___ j'ai besoin, ce sont des vacances.
cards.note: If the verb takes the preposition de, use ce dont: avoir besoin de, parler de, rêver de.

cards.task: Add emphasis using ce que … c'est.
cards.answer: Ce que je préfère, c'est le fromage.
cards.note: The pattern is ce que + subject + verb, c'est + object. The comma before c'est is standard.

cards.de: I'm the one who is right, not you.
cards.fr: C'est moi qui a raison, pas toi.
cards.answer: C'est moi qui ai raison, pas toi.
cards.note: A classic slip is putting the verb in the third person. After c'est moi qui the verb agrees with the first person: qui ai.

cards.de: It was in Lyon that I grew up.
cards.fr: C'est à Lyon où j'ai grandi.
cards.answer: C'est à Lyon que j'ai grandi.
cards.note: When you highlight a place or a time, the linker is always que, never où or quand: c'est demain que, c'est ici que.

cards.de: It's the children who tidied the room.
cards.answer: Ce sont les enfants qui ont rangé la chambre.
accept: C'est les enfants qui ont rangé la chambre.
cards.note: Before a plural noun, careful French uses ce sont. C'est les enfants is only heard in casual speech.

cards.de: What I don't understand is why he said nothing.
cards.answer: Ce que je ne comprends pas, c'est pourquoi il n'a rien dit.
accept: Ce que je ne comprends pas, c'est pourquoi il n'a rien dit du tout.
cards.note: A whole clause can follow c'est, exactly as English follows "is" with "why he said nothing".

cards.de: It's the neighbours who are making the noise.
cards.fr: ___ les voisins qui font du bruit.
cards.note: This structure uses ce, never il or ils. With a plural noun the correct form is ce sont.

cards.de: This is the film I saw, not the other one.
cards.fr: C'est ce film ___ j'ai vu, pas l'autre.
cards.note: When the highlighted element is the object, use c'est … que. Only a highlighted subject takes c'est … qui.

cards.de: Personally, I don't find that funny.
cards.answer: Moi, je ne trouve pas ça drôle.
accept: Moi, je ne trouve pas cela drôle.
cards.note: The simplest way to add emphasis is the doubled pronoun: moi, je … / toi, tu … It works like English "personally, I …" or a stressed "I".

cards.de: He is rich, whereas his brother is poor.
cards.fr: Il est riche, ___ son frère est pauvre.
cards.note: pendant que is purely about time (during the period when). tandis que and alors que can also express a contrast.

Donc and car are opposites in direction: donc gives the result of the rain, car gives the reason for coming home. Même si and puisque both introduce a clause but même si concedes a hypothesis, while puisque states a fact both speakers already know; alors que here contrasts two simultaneous actions.

cards.de: Since you're already here, you can help me.
cards.fr: ___ tu es déjà là, tu peux m'aider.
cards.note: puisque gives a reason the listener already knows. parce que gives new information and usually follows the main clause, while car simply links two main clauses.

cards.de: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.
cards.fr: Je parle lentement afin que tout le monde ___.
cards.note: afin que and pour que are always followed by the subjonctif. Note that tout le monde is grammatically singular.

cards.de: Instead of watching TV all evening, you could read a book.
cards.fr: Au lieu de tu regardes la télé, tu pourrais lire un livre.
cards.answer: Au lieu de regarder la télé, tu pourrais lire un livre.
accept: Au lieu de regarder la télé toute la soirée, tu pourrais lire un livre.
cards.note: au lieu de is followed by an infinitive, never by a conjugated verb. Only when the two subjects differ do you use au lieu que plus subjonctif.

cards.de: He studied a lot. Even so, he didn't pass the exam.
cards.answer: Il a beaucoup travaillé. Pourtant, il n'a pas réussi l'examen.
accept: Il a beaucoup étudié. Pourtant, il n'a pas réussi l'examen.
Il a beaucoup travaillé. Il n'a pourtant pas réussi l'examen.
cards.note: pourtant means "even so" and sits at the start of the sentence or right before the past participle. It is an adverb, so the word order stays normal.

cards.de: The first film was terrible. The second one, on the other hand, was excellent.
cards.fr: Le premier film était nul. ___, le deuxième était excellent.
cards.note: en revanche contrasts two things and sounds more written than par contre. It introduces a full main clause of its own.

cards.de: Since it was raining, we stayed at home.
cards.fr: Nous sommes restés à la maison, comme il pleuvait.
cards.answer: Comme il pleuvait, nous sommes restés à la maison.
cards.note: When comme means "since", it almost always opens the sentence. To put the reason second, use parce que or car.

cards.de: I'm calling you to warn you.
cards.note: When both halves share the same subject, use afin de plus an infinitive. afin que plus subjonctif is only needed when the subject changes.

cards.fr: Il est parti tôt parce qu'il voulait éviter les embouteillages.
cards.task: Express the reason as a purpose with afin de.
cards.answer: Il est parti tôt afin d'éviter les embouteillages.
accept: Il est parti tôt afin d'éviter les bouchons.
cards.note: Since the subject is the same in both halves, the clause becomes an infinitive. Before a vowel, afin de becomes afin d'.

cards.fr: Tu ne fais rien. Tu devrais chercher du travail.
cards.task: Join the two sentences with au lieu de.
cards.answer: Au lieu de ne rien faire, tu devrais chercher du travail.
accept: Au lieu de ne rien faire, tu devrais chercher un travail.
cards.note: With an infinitive, ne and rien stand together in front of it: ne rien faire. That keeps the negation inside the infinitive phrase.

cards.de: She accepted the job even though she didn't like the work.
cards.fr: Elle a accepté le poste ___ ce travail ne lui plaisait pas.
cards.note: alors que can mark simultaneity but also a strong contrast ("whereas", "even though"). It always takes the indicatif, never the subjonctif.

cards.de: Since I don't have a car, I take the train.
cards.hint: reason first, at the start of the sentence
cards.answer: Comme je n'ai pas de voiture, je prends le train.
accept: Puisque je n'ai pas de voiture, je prends le train.
cards.note: comme at the start of a sentence means "since" or "as" and gives the reason. After a negative, un/une becomes de: pas de voiture.

cards.de: My grandmother is ninety-seven years old.
cards.note: Built as 4 times 20 plus 17. In Belgium and Switzerland people say nonante-sept.
Cent takes an s in deux cents but loses it again in deux cent un, because a number follows. Mille never takes an s, and million needs an article: un million.
21, 31 and 71 take et with no hyphens, but 81 and 91 do not: quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze. Quatre-vingts takes an s only when nothing follows it.
vingt takes an s in quatre-vingts, but loses it when another number follows: quatre-vingt-deux.
71 is built as 60 plus 11. The et appears in 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71.

cards.de: The book has two hundred pages.
cards.note: cent takes an s in the plural when no further number follows it.

cards.de: The bike costs three hundred and fifty euros.
cards.note: Here cent stays without an s because another number follows.

cards.de: The town has twenty thousand inhabitants.
cards.note: mille never changes and never takes an s.

cards.de: The country has six million inhabitants.
cards.fr: Le pays a six millions habitants.
cards.answer: Le pays a six millions d'habitants.
cards.note: million and milliard are nouns, so they need de before the following noun. Note also that French keeps the plural s: six millions.

cards.de: The price has gone up by 2.5 percent.
cards.fr: Le prix a augmenté de deux ___ cinq pour cent.
cards.note: French uses a comma where English uses a decimal point, and it is read aloud as virgule.

cards.de: A third of the inhabitants are under twenty.
cards.answer: Un tiers des habitants a moins de vingt ans.
accept: Un tiers des habitants ont moins de vingt ans.
cards.note: Fractions: un tiers, un quart, then from five on un cinquième, un sixième. The verb after un tiers stays singular.

cards.answer: La moitié des élèves était malade.
accept: La moitié des élèves étaient malades.
cards.note: "Half" as a noun is la moitié; demi is the adjective, as in une demi-heure.

cards.de: She lives on the ninth floor.
cards.note: Ordinals end in -ième. neuf changes f to v, and cinq adds a u: cinquième.

cards.de: Can you give me your phone number?
cards.fr: Tu peux me donner ton ___ de téléphone ?
cards.note: le numéro is a number used as a label or identifier; le nombre is a quantity or amount.

cards.de: There were about twenty people at the party.
cards.fr: Il y avait ___ à la fête.
cards.note: The ending -aine gives an approximate quantity: une dizaine, une quinzaine, une centaine. It is always followed by de.
81 and 91 take no et. The et only appears in 21 through 71.
Only the first of the month uses an ordinal: le premier mai, but le deux mai, le trois mai.
Apart from the first, dates always use cardinal numbers: le huit octobre, le vingt mars. Ordinals like huitième are wrong here.
Unlike English, French writes months and weekdays with a small letter. No comma before the year.

cards.de: What time does the film start?
cards.answer: À quelle heure commence le film ?
accept: À quelle heure est-ce que le film commence ?
Le film commence à quelle heure ?
cards.note: You ask about clock time with à quelle heure. A time of day always takes à: à huit heures.
French never drops heures, so you cannot just say "quarter past eight". Quarter past is et quart, half past is et demie.
For times before the hour you name the coming hour and use moins, and the quarter takes an article: sept heures moins le quart.
demi agrees with the word it refers to. After the masculine midi and minuit it stays demi, but after heures it becomes demie.

cards.answer: Le train part à dix-neuf heures quarante-cinq.
cards.note: Timetables use the official 24-hour clock with plain numbers. It is written 19 h 45, not 19:45.
Years and months take en: en 2015, en mai. English "in" here is never dans.

cards.de: On Monday I have an appointment at the dentist's.
cards.answer: Lundi, j'ai un rendez-vous chez le dentiste.
accept: J'ai un rendez-vous chez le dentiste lundi.
Lundi j'ai un rendez-vous chez le dentiste.
cards.note: A single day of the week needs no article and no preposition. "On Monday" is simply lundi.

cards.de: The library is closed on Mondays.
cards.note: With the article, the weekday expresses a habit: le lundi means on Mondays, every Monday.
un bouchon is just as common in informal speech (literally a cork).
Feminine. The h is silent, hence l'habitude and d'habitude (usually).
Masculine despite the -e ending. Words in -aire are usually masculine: le dictionnaire, l'anniversaire.
Typically used in a pair: certes ..., mais ... Certes, c'est cher, mais la qualité est excellente. (Admittedly it is expensive, but the quality is excellent.) Slightly more formal than bien sûr.
Common in set phrases: c'est bien fait (well done) and c'est bien fait pour toi (it serves you right).
Feminine, and not to be confused with the verb form il tombe (he falls). A gravestone is la pierre tombale.
The same word also works as an adjective: tomber malade means to fall ill.
The masculine plural is irregular: sociaux, feminine sociale. Very common: les réseaux sociaux.
Reflexive s'établir means to settle down. Common uses: établir un contact, établir une liste.
Watch the spelling: one l but double o. It sounds like "alkol".
Built as surgir de quelque part, for example surgir de l'ombre. Takes avoir in the passé composé.
Note the circumflex on the o. Used as a modifier with no hyphen: une ville fantôme.
Without an article, samedi means this coming Saturday; with le, le samedi means on Saturdays.
Nouns ending in té are almost always feminine. It covers both a unit of measurement and unity in the sense of togetherness.

cards.de: to undergo, to suffer (something done to you)
cards.note: Takes a direct object: subir une opération, subir une défaite. The subject is on the receiving end.

cards.de: to cross, to get past (a line, a stage)
cards.note: No preposition needed: franchir la ligne, franchir une étape. Don't mix it up with français.
Plural niveaux. Very common in au niveau de, meaning at the level of or as regards.
Feminine doubles the n: mignonne. Also used to mean kind: sois mignon, aide-moi.
Built as lier quelque chose à quelque chose. Se lier d'amitié avec quelqu'un means to strike up a friendship.
Feminine form: brillante. It comes from the verb briller, to shine.
provoquer un accident, provoquer une réaction. It can also mean to provoke someone.
As in l'Empire romain. The related noun is l'empereur, the emperor.
Il y avait environ vingt personnes à la réunion. (There were about twenty people at the meeting.) Don't confuse it with les environs, the surrounding area.
Same form in the masculine and feminine. There is also a verb tendre, to stretch or hold out: tendre la main à qn.
Masculine. Common phrases: se mettre à l'abri, to get to safety, and à l'abri de la pluie.
Plural: les adieux. dire adieu à qn means goodbye for good; otherwise use au revoir.
Masculine. Nouns in -é are usually masculine (le café, le degré), while nouns in -té are feminine. le comité d'entreprise is a works council.
J'ai un bleu au bras. The same word also means the colour blue and, informally, a newcomer.
contrôler les billets = to check the tickets. It also means to have control over: se contrôler = to control oneself.
Feminine form: sure. Don't confuse it with sûr (sure, certain, with the accent) or with the preposition sur (on).
Either goûter qc or goûter à qc. As a noun, le goûter is the afternoon snack.
Same form for masculine and feminine. Adverb: honnêtement (honestly, to be honest).
It often comes before the noun: un vaste projet, une vaste plaine. The feminine form is identical.
Always reflexive: dépêche-toi ! Before an infinitive it takes de: se dépêcher de finir.
With manquer the person you miss is the subject, so the sentence is literally "my sister is lacking to me".
connaître is for people, places and things you are familiar with; savoir is for facts and clauses: je sais qu'il est bon.

cards.de: I have been living in Lyon for three years.
cards.note: depuis covers a period still going on now. il y a trois ans means three years ago, pendant trois ans means for three years (finished).

cards.de: I have reserved a seat on the train.
cards.fr: J'ai réservé une ___ dans le train.
cards.note: la place is a seat or the space something takes up. un endroit and un lieu mean a location or spot.

cards.de: I am looking for a flat.
cards.note: chercher takes a direct object with no preposition, unlike English "look for". Same with attendre le bus and demander l'addition.

cards.fr: Elle se rappelle de mon nom.
cards.note: se rappeler quelque chose takes no de, while se souvenir does: elle se souvient de mon nom.

cards.de: I feel like going to the cinema tonight.
cards.answer: J'ai envie d'aller au cinéma ce soir.
accept: Ce soir, j'ai envie d'aller au cinéma.
cards.note: avoir envie de plus an infinitive means to feel like doing something. With a noun: j'ai envie d'un café.

cards.fr: Tu dois partir tout de suite.
cards.answer: Il faut que tu partes tout de suite.
accept: Il faut que tu partes tout de suite !
cards.note: il faut que is followed by the subjonctif. partir gives que tu partes.
Construction: fournir qc à qn. L'école fournit les livres aux élèves. (The school provides the books to the students.) Also common in fournir un effort (to make an effort).
réserver une table pour deux. Reflexive se réserver qc means to save something for oneself.
Before the noun it is hyphenated and never changes: une demi-heure. After the noun it agrees: une heure et demie.
Irregular past participle of voir. Set phrases: bien vu (well regarded), vu que (given that, since).
Feminine noun. Common phrases: en pleine saison, les quatre saisons.
Irregular feminine form: inquiète. Construction: être inquiet pour qn (to be worried about someone).
Nouns ending in -ion are almost always feminine in French. Example: dans la région de Lyon.
Usually used in the plural: les fesses (the bottom). It is informal; in a medical context you hear le fessier.
Colloquial alternative to rire. On a bien rigolé pendant le repas. (We had a good laugh during the meal.) Tu rigoles ! means You're kidding!
Feminine form: brune. For brown objects use marron, which does not change form.
It also means a written character or letter: en gros caractères. Avoir bon caractère means to be easy-going.
Spelled the same in singular and plural, and the s is silent. Le tapis roulant is a treadmill or a conveyor belt.

cards.de: hot, warm (as in: it is hot, I am hot)
cards.note: It stays unchanged after avoir and faire: j'ai chaud, il fait chaud. Never say être chaud about a person, as it suggests being aroused.
The same form works for masculine and feminine. Capitalised as a noun: un Russe (a Russian).

cards.de: the farmer, the peasant (person working the land)
cards.note: Feminine form: paysanne. It can sound slightly disparaging; un agriculteur is the neutral word.
The final t is silent, but you hear it in the feminine lente. Adverb: lentement.
Feminine form of maître. It also means a primary school teacher, which is what children call her.

cards.de: a thousand (a group of about a thousand)
cards.note: Mostly used in the plural: des milliers de personnes. After millier comes de with no article.
Faire le portrait de qn can also mean to describe someone in words.
Conjugated like couvrir: je recouvre, j'ai recouvert. Construction: recouvrir qc de qc.

cards.de: to accomplish, to carry out (a task)
cards.note: Regular -ir verb like finir: j'accomplis, nous accomplissons. Common: accomplir une tâche, accomplir son devoir.

cards.de: the commissioner, the superintendent (senior police officer)
cards.note: Same form for a woman: la commissaire. Typical phrase: commissaire de police.

cards.de: to make sure of, to see to it (take care that)
cards.note: Veiller à qc, veiller à ce que + subjonctif. Je veille à ce que tout soit prêt avant midi. (I make sure everything is ready before noon.) Veiller sur qn means to watch over someone.
Dépasser les limites means to go too far. À la limite is colloquial for if need be, at a pinch.

cards.de: to perfect, to put the finishing touches to
cards.note: Conjugated like faire, but used almost only in the infinitive. Elle est partie en Espagne pour parfaire son espagnol. (She left for Spain to perfect her Spanish.)
Feminine form suivante: la page suivante. Au suivant! is what you hear in a queue: next, please.

cards.de: to bring closer, to bring together
cards.note: Very common as a reflexive: se rapprocher de qn/qc. Ce voyage nous a rapprochés. (That trip brought us closer together.)
Refaire surface means to resurface or turn up again. Une grande surface is a supermarket.
Feminine réelle, adverb réellement. Le monde réel is the opposite of the virtual world.
Feminine nulle. Also match nul, a draw, and nulle part, nowhere.
J'ai déchiré la lettre sans la lire. (I tore up the letter without reading it.) Se déchirer un muscle means to tear a muscle. Ça déchire ! is slang for that's awesome.

cards.de: to annoy, to get on someone's nerves (vulgar)
cards.note: Vulgar, derived from merde, so avoid it with strangers. Arrête de m'emmerder avec tes questions ! (Stop bugging me with your questions!) S'emmerder means to be bored out of your mind.

cards.de: the investigation, the inquiry (by the police)
cards.note: Feminine. Mener or ouvrir une enquête sur qc. Also a survey: une enquête d'opinion.
Past participle of arriver, which takes être and agrees with the subject. Le train est arrivé avec vingt minutes de retard. (The train arrived twenty minutes late.)
Conjugated like battre: je combats, nous combattons. The object follows directly, with no preposition: combattre le racisme.
affirmer que + indicative. Il affirme qu'il n'a rien vu. (He claims he saw nothing.) The opposite is nier (to deny).
Comparative of mauvais: pire = worse, le pire = the worst. Common: le pire, c'est que ...

cards.de: to attach (e.g. a file to an email)
cards.note: Irregular: je joins, nous joignons, participle joint. Joindre qn also means to reach someone by phone.
Masculine despite the -e ending. Common: C'est un mystère pour moi.
je conclus, participle conclu. Les deux entreprises ont conclu un accord hier. (The two companies reached an agreement yesterday.)
Spelled just like the English word, but pronounced steel. Le style de vie means lifestyle.
Feminine: particulière. en particulier = in particular; un cours particulier = a private lesson.
Feminine: soudaine, e.g. une mort soudaine. The same form also works as an adverb: Soudain, il s'est levé.
Very often reflexive: se précipiter vers qn. Elle s'est précipitée vers la sortie. (She rushed towards the exit.) Ne rien précipiter means not to rush anything.

cards.de: knowledge (the body of what is known)
cards.note: An infinitive used as a noun, so it is masculine. le savoir = knowledge in general, les connaissances = the things you know.
être mort de fatigue = to be dead tired. The related adjective is fatigué.
Le professeur rassemble les élèves dans la cour. (The teacher gathers the students in the playground.) se rassembler = to gather (of people); rassembler ses idées = to collect one's thoughts.
faire sa prière = to say one's prayers. On signs, prière de ... means please do (or please do not).
Feminine: obscure. Also figurative: un passage obscur = an unclear passage in a text.
Feminine. l'opinion publique = public opinion. But to give your own view, the usual phrase is à mon avis.
je réduis, past participle réduit. réduire qc de moitié = to cut something by half.

cards.de: to accustom, to get (someone) used to
cards.note: habituer qn à qc; reflexive s'habituer à qc = to get used to something. Je me suis habitué à me lever tôt. (I got used to getting up early.) Also avoir l'habitude de faire qc.

cards.de: fed up (in: en avoir ... de qc = to be sick of something)
cards.note: Used only in the expression en avoir marre, and it is informal. J'en ai marre de ce travail. (I am fed up with this job.)
Feminine: la prisonnière. prendre qn prisonnier = to take someone prisoner.
From expliquer. Common: donner une explication à qn. avoir une explication avec qn means to have it out with someone.
Also a mark or trace: les marques de doigts = fingerprints. une grande marque = a well known brand.
The final t is silent. Informally, prendre un pot = to go for a drink.
Irregular: je résous, nous résolvons, participle résolu. résoudre un problème.
Regular -er verb, takes avoir. La bombe a explosé près de la gare. (The bomb exploded near the station.) Figurative: exploser de colère = to explode with anger.

Past participle of fermer, used as an adjective and agreeing in gender and number. La boulangerie est fermée le lundi. (The bakery is closed on Mondays.) Of people: il est très fermé = he keeps himself to himself.

Also to recapture or to make up: rattraper son retard = to make up lost time. Cours, tu peux encore le rattraper ! (Run, you can still catch up with him!) se rattraper = to catch oneself, to make up for it.
Same form for masculine and feminine. Pattern: être utile à qn (to be useful to someone).
Nouns ending in -esse are always feminine. Related to the adjective tendre (tender, soft).
Ce bruit m'énerve depuis ce matin. (That noise has been annoying me since this morning.) Tu m'énerves ! is very common. Reflexive s'énerver means to get worked up.
Louer covers both renting from someone and renting out, so context decides. Nous louons un appartement près de la plage. (We are renting a flat near the beach.) A second meaning is to praise.
Feminine, and the source of the English word. Common: une silhouette élancée (a slender figure).
Masculine plural is égaux, feminine égale. Ça m'est égal = I don't mind.
Masculine, like most nouns in -oire with this meaning. Sur le territoire français.

cards.de: the vision, the view (way of seeing)
cards.note: Nouns ending in -sion are always feminine. Sa vision des choses = his view of things.
Conjugated like courir: je parcours, participe parcouru. Also to skim: parcourir un texte.
Same form for both genders. Stronger than beau and very common in praise: une vue superbe.
An old coin, now mostly in set phrases: ne pas avoir un sou = to be penniless.
Belongs to souffrir (to suffer). Common: souffrance physique, être en souffrance.
Ends in -e and is feminine. Careful: la datte with two t's is the fruit, a date.
The ending -ique stays the same in both genders. Capitalised as a noun: un Britannique.
It also means a spot or pimple, and a bud: un bouton de rose.
Feminine vaine. Very common in the phrase en vain (in vain).
The final c is pronounced. Common: un parc d'attractions (theme park).
Pattern: désigner qn comme responsable. On l'a désigné comme responsable du projet. (They appointed him as head of the project.) It also means to point at something.
Also used for flags in the wind. Le bateau en papier flotte encore sur l'eau. (The paper boat is still floating on the water.) Colloquially: il flotte, it's raining.
Feminine: une étudiante. Use en for the subject: étudiant en droit.
From tuer (to kill); feminine la tueuse. Common: un tueur en série (a serial killer).
Feminine violente. It also works for things: une violente tempête.
From chasser (to hunt). In a hotel, le chasseur is the bellboy.
Feminine plate. De l'eau plate means still water.
Feminine éternelle with a double l. Adverb: éternellement.
Feminine: sourde. Common: être sourd d'une oreille; un bruit sourd is a dull, muffled noise.
Same form for masculine and feminine. Polite: C'est très agréable de vous revoir.
Feminine noun. Common: avoir de l'imagination (to be imaginative).
In the plural, les urgences means A&E / the emergency room. Also d'urgence = urgently, immediately.
Feminine noun. Common: une série télévisée; en série = mass-produced.
Masculine despite the -e ending. Common: un cercle d'amis; en cercle = in a circle.
In casual speech super is also an invariable adjective: c'est super = that's great.
Usually used in the singular. From nourrir (to feed).
As an adjective the form does not change for gender: une idée vague. Do not confuse it with la vague = the wave.
Feminine: une infirmière, very common. Workplace: à l'hôpital.

cards.de: to note down, to write down
cards.note: Also to mark or grade work (noter un devoir). Common: noter qc dans son agenda.
Very colloquial; the neutral word is manger. J'ai envie de bouffer un truc rapide. [I feel like grabbing something quick to eat.] Related: la bouffe = grub, food.
Nationalities as people take a capital R; the language is lower case and masculine: le russe. Feminine: une Russe.
Verb: assassiner qn. Stronger than meurtrier: it suggests a planned killing.
A masculine noun. Common phrase: être en état de choc, to be in shock.
Masculine plural principaux, feminine principale. Le principal means the main thing.
Masculine despite the -e ending, like le problème. Common: au programme, on the programme.

cards.de: the task (a job to be done)
cards.note: The circumflex matters: without it, la tache means a stain.
Masculine despite the -e ending. Common: aller au cimetière.
Also means material or matter: les matières premières are raw materials. En matière de means as regards.
Used of people (very thin), of meat, and figuratively: un maigre salaire, a meagre wage.

cards.de: the true (as a noun: what is true)
cards.note: An adjective used as a noun. Very common in à vrai dire, to tell the truth.
Also means a quill or pen nib. Léger comme une plume means light as a feather.
Feminine form une ouvrière. It means a manual worker in a factory or on a site, not just anyone with a job.
Il ne sert à rien de soupirer, il faut agir. [There is no point sighing, you have to act.] The noun is un soupir. Soupirer après qc means to long for something.
A masculine noun. À l'horizon means on the horizon.
Les soldats ont commencé à envahir le pays voisin. [The soldiers began to invade the neighbouring country.] Takes a direct object. Conjugated like finir (nous envahissons); the noun is une invasion.
Passer la frontière means to cross the border. An abstract boundary is usually une limite.
