Figuratively: c'est toujours le même refrain, it's always the same old story.
Identical in form to the past participle of revenir. Plural les revenus means earnings; impôt sur le revenu is income tax.
Conjugated like conduire: je reconduis, nous reconduisons. A second sense is to renew a mandate or an agreement. Je vais te reconduire chez toi en voiture. (I'll take you back home by car.)
Typical collocation: distribuer des tracts. Do not confuse it with le contrat.
Always written with a hyphen and unchanged in the plural. The opposite is le mal-être.
In France it usually means a speed camera: se faire prendre par un radar.
The final s is pronounced: [vis]. Spelled the same as vis from vivre or voir; serrer une vis.
The butcher is le boucher. Figuratively, boucherie also means slaughter or carnage.
Tent pegs are des piquets de tente. A piquet de grève is a picket line.
Feminine form découverte. The phrase à découvert means exposed or in the red; le découvert is an overdraft.
Don't confuse it with le procès (a trial) or la procédure (procedure, the steps followed).

cards.de: to postpone (move an appointment to later)
cards.note: Used as reporter qc à plus tard. The noun le reporter (reporter) is pronounced the English way.
Feminine form indiscrète. Opposite: discret; une question indiscrète is a prying question.
Common uses: un véhicule blindé, une porte blindée. Colloquially blindé also means packed full.

cards.de: the distinction (making a difference between things)
cards.note: Nouns ending in -tion are always feminine. A second meaning is an award or refined manner.
Un tampon encreur is an ink stamp. Depending on context the word also means buffer or tampon.
Only used reflexively: se vautrer dans le canapé. Colloquial and slightly disapproving.

cards.de: the assistant (junior employee in a shop or kitchen)
cards.note: Slightly old-fashioned; today mostly in un commis de cuisine. The final s is silent.
Used as coopérer avec qn à qc. The two o's are pronounced separately: ko-opérer. Notre équipe coopère avec une entreprise allemande. (Our team is cooperating with a German company.)
Nouns ending in -ence are feminine. Set phrase: en toute transparence, completely openly.

For emphasis: trempé jusqu'aux os, soaked to the bone. Of steel, trempé means tempered. Je suis rentré trempé parce que j'avais oublié mon parapluie. (I came home soaked because I had forgotten my umbrella.)
Written with a single n, unlike English tyrant with its t. The related noun la tyrannie has two n's.

cards.de: to overshadow (to outshine, put in the shade)
cards.note: From une éclipse, an eclipse. Reflexive s'éclipser means to slip away quietly. Son succès a complètement éclipsé celui des autres. (Her success completely overshadowed that of the others.)
Feminine form républicaine. As a noun, un républicain means a Republican.
It is sous plus coupe, the dish underneath. Une soucoupe volante is a flying saucer.
Very common in de l'eau minérale. The masculine plural is irregular: minéraux.
Feminine, like every word ending in -tion. Often used in the plural: des complications après l'opération.
Do not mix it up with impossible. A typical phrase is rester impassible, to keep a straight face.
It already ends in -e, so the feminine form is identical. Works for people and things alike: une santé robuste.
Ce tableau est trop abstrait pour moi. (This painting is too abstract for me.) Feminine: abstraite, where the t becomes audible. The opposite is concret.
The counterpart of une blonde. Une brune is also a dark beer.
Formed from nouveau. Nouns ending in -té are regularly feminine.
Typical uses: les pneus crissent, le gravier crisse sous les pas.
One form for both genders: un/une pensionnaire. It also means a lodger or a resident in a care home.

Je collabore avec Marie à ce projet. (I am working together with Marie on this project.) The pattern is collaborer avec qn à qc. The noun collaborateur also carries the historical sense of wartime collaborator.
Le petit prince a apprivoisé le renard. (The little prince tamed the fox.) For wild animals in a circus you say dompter instead.
J'ai trop mangé, j'ai envie de gerber. (I ate too much, I feel like puking.) Very colloquial; the neutral verb is vomir. In technical language gerber also means to stack goods.
Je présume qu'il est déjà parti. (I presume he has already left.) Takes présumer que plus the indicative. Familiar from présumé innocent, presumed innocent.
Same form for women: une arbitre. Le libre arbitre means free will.
From habile, skilful. Do not confuse it with habilité, which means official authorisation.
Typical phrase: une liasse de billets, a wad of banknotes.
Feminine musulmane, plural musulmans. Unlike English, it stays lowercase even as a noun: un musulman.
Cette chanson me trotte dans la tête depuis ce matin. (I can't get this song out of my head since this morning.) Literally it means to trot, and it is also used of people who are always on the go.
Tu es tenu de prévenir ton patron. (You are obliged to inform your boss.) Used in the construction être tenu de faire qc. Do not confuse it with ténu, meaning very thin or faint.

cards.de: the platform (raised area in a room)
cards.note: Feminine. Typically the low platform in front of a classroom blackboard, not a theatre stage, which is la scène.
The plural is regular: des festivals, not festivaux.
Feminine frisée: des cheveux frisés, une perruque frisée. La frisée is also a type of curly endive.
Also figurative: sceller un pacte, to seal an alliance. Do not confuse it with seller, to saddle, which sounds identical.
Typical use: la région a été ravagée par les incendies. Like all -ger verbs it keeps an e before a and o: nous ravageons.
Colloquial, feminine une rouquine. The neutral word is un roux.
Feminine hardie. It sounds rather formal, often in un projet hardi or une remarque hardie.
The same word covers optics: des lentilles de contact means contact lenses.
Le Massif central is the Central Massif in France. Un massif de fleurs, by contrast, is a flower bed.
Nous avons attendu patiemment pendant deux heures. (We waited patiently for two hours.) Pronounced pa-sya-man, because adjectives ending in -ent take the ending -emment.
Feminine une voyante, often used for fortune tellers. Un voyant lumineux is also a warning light in a car.
Common in technical and medical contexts: détecter une fuite, une maladie. Related noun: un détecteur de fumée, a smoke detector.
All nouns ending in -ité are feminine. Common phrase: avec une rapidité surprenante.
As an adjective sage usually means well behaved: sois sage! Only as a noun does it mean a wise person.
An English borrowing, masculine in French. Colloquial: il a changé de look, he changed his look.

cards.de: the sign (board with writing on it)
cards.note: A board or placard with text, for example at a demonstration. A road sign is un panneau.
It describes a sequence: il a occupé successivement trois postes. It never means at the same time.

cards.de: what has been said (the spoken word)
cards.note: Rare as a noun, almost only in le dit et le non-dit, what is said and what is left unsaid. Usually dit is the participle of dire.
Un whisky avec des glaçons. Nouns ending in -on are nearly always masculine.
Feminine form majestueuse. Typically used of landscapes and buildings: un paysage majestueux.
Masculine: le bungalow. In France it often means a small holiday cabin on a campsite.
Feminine and rather formal: une entrevue entre les deux présidents. A job interview is un entretien.
All nouns ending in -té are feminine. Often avec lucidité, or a lucid moment in someone who is ill.
On a édifié cette cathédrale au treizième siècle. (This cathedral was erected in the thirteenth century.) More formal than construire. Also figurative: édifier une théorie, to build up a theory.
Only used for a child's school bag. A rucksack is le sac à dos.
Adjectives ending in -iste do not change in the feminine: un projet réaliste, une vision réaliste.
Il est strictement interdit de fumer ici. (It is strictly forbidden to smoke here.) Very common in that phrase and in strictement nécessaire.
Also tic nerveux. A verbal habit is un tic de langage.
From la grimace. The c becomes ç before a and o: nous grimaçons, il grimaçait.
The short form la gym is very colloquial and often means PE at school.
Ses amis l'influencent beaucoup. (His friends influence him a lot.) influencer qn takes a direct object, with no preposition. Before a and o: nous influençons.
It also means looking something up: la consultation d'un dictionnaire.
Masculine despite the -e ending. For nuns you normally say le couvent.
In France people say centime rather than cent. Set phrase: ça ne coûte pas un centime, it doesn't cost a penny.
Feminine: la romancière. From le roman, which means novel, not romance.
Feminine: la métamorphose. The verb is se métamorphoser en qc, to turn into something.
Same form for both genders: un hôpital psychiatrique, une clinique psychiatrique.
Colloquial and slightly old-fashioned. The verb épater qn means to amaze someone.
From la griffe, a claw: Le chat m'a griffé. To scratch yourself is se gratter.
Il astique ses chaussures avant chaque entretien. (He polishes his shoes before every interview.) Everyday word for thorough, rub until shiny cleaning.
répartir qc entre plusieurs personnes. Don't confuse it with repartir, to set off again.
Almost only in à la tombée de la nuit, at nightfall.
Feminine: la syllabe. Useful phrase: un mot de deux syllabes.
Ce filtre purifie l'eau du robinet. (This filter purifies the tap water.) Used with l'eau or l'air. Reflexive se purifier means to cleanse oneself inwardly.
Feminine form vicieuse. Very common in un cercle vicieux, a vicious circle.
Almost only in être à l'affût de qc, to be on the lookout for something.
A shade more formal than politesse. Phrase: par courtoisie, out of courtesy.
Takes a direct object: esquiver un coup, une question. s'esquiver means to slip away unnoticed.
Capitalised as a noun, lower case as an adjective: le vin autrichien. Feminine: une Autrichienne.
figé sur place, rooted to the spot. An expression figée is a set phrase.
Informally shortened to l'apéro. Phrase: prendre l'apéritif.
Ma grand-mère nous contait des histoires le soir. (My grandmother used to tell us stories in the evening.) Literary, related to le conte, a fairy tale. It sounds exactly like compter, to count.
Ce thé est trop sucré pour moi. (This tea is too sweet for me.) The classic pair is sucré and salé. For sweet meaning cute, use mignon.
Used practically only reflexively, as in tapi dans l'ombre, lurking in the shadows. Example: Le renard se tapit derrière les buissons. (The fox crouches behind the bushes.)
The same word works as an adjective: une situation explosive.
Le prof a rectifié mon erreur au tableau. (The teacher corrected my mistake on the board.) Figuratively rectifier le tir means to adjust one's approach.
Elle vit séparée de son mari depuis un an. (She has been living apart from her husband for a year.) Used as séparé de qn or qc. Of couples: ils vivent séparés, they live apart.

cards.de: to clink, to tinkle (a bright sound, like glasses)
cards.note: les verres tintent, faire tinter une clochette. Do not confuse it with teinter, to tint.
Formed from volontaire. Il a volontairement oublié de m'inviter. (He deliberately forgot to invite me.) The opposite is involontairement, unintentionally.
Feminine: la défunte. More formal than le mort and typical of obituaries.
Watch the spelling: the adjective is fatigant without u, the present participle fatiguant with u. Not the same as fatigué, tired.
Built from ferme. Common combinations: croire fermement, refuser fermement.

cards.de: to break, to surge in (of waves)
cards.note: Les vagues déferlent sur la plage. Also figurative for crowds: la foule déferle dans la rue.
Used as propice à qc. Le moment propice is the right moment.

cards.de: the shorts, the pair of shorts
cards.note: French treats it as a singular masculine noun: un short, deux shorts. Borrowed from English.
The ending -emment is pronounced like amant. Elle voit les choses différemment de moi. (She sees things differently from me.) Often followed by de.
Ne t'inquiète pas, je blague! (Don't worry, I'm joking!) Colloquial. Very common: sans blague!, no kidding?
Son sourire a charmé tout le monde. (Her smile charmed everyone.) charmer qn, with no preposition. The original sense was to cast a spell, hence un charmeur de serpents, a snake charmer.
Il dédaigne les gens qui n'ont pas étudié. (He scorns people who have not studied.) dédaigner qn/qc takes a direct object, no preposition. The noun is le dédain, contempt.

cards.de: to tread on, to set foot on
cards.note: Neil Armstrong a foulé le sol de la Lune en 1969. (Neil Armstrong set foot on the Moon in 1969.) Often used as fouler le sol. Reflexive se fouler la cheville means to sprain your ankle.
From the verb hésiter à faire qc, to hesitate to do something. Feminine: hésitante.
Feminine: gourmande. Not the same as gourmet: a gourmand eats a lot, a gourmet eats well.
From the verb bouillir. Typical: de l'eau bouillante.
Feminine: fâcheuse. Rather formal, often in un fâcheux contretemps or c'est fâcheux.
From vain, futile. J'ai vainement cherché mes clés pendant une heure. (I searched in vain for my keys for an hour.) In everyday speech people usually say en vain.
Typical combination: donneur de sang. Feminine form: la donneuse.
Feminine: impérieuse. Also used to mean urgent: un besoin impérieux.
The c becomes ç before a and o to keep the soft sound: nous finançons, il finançait.

cards.de: the good guy (the good character in a film)
cards.note: Its counterpart is le méchant. As an adjective, gentil means nice or kind, feminine gentille.
Usually appears with l': faire l'inverse, and à l'inverse de means unlike or contrary to. The noun is masculine.

cards.de: the neon light, the neon tube
cards.note: Also the gas neon. Common phrase: la lumière des néons.
Feminine: tardive. Common: à une heure tardive, un dîner tardif.
From prudent; like évidemment, the emm is pronounced "amman". Il neige, alors conduis prudemment. (It is snowing, so drive carefully.)
Elle rayonne de joie depuis l'annonce. (She has been beaming with joy since the announcement.) From le rayon, a ray.

cards.de: blood- (relating to blood, e.g. blood group)
cards.note: Used in le groupe sanguin and un vaisseau sanguin. Of people it means hot-tempered.
The final s is silent and the singular and plural look the same. Le vernis à ongles is nail polish.
S'infecter means to become infected, of a wound. Ne touche pas la plaie, elle risque de s'infecter. (Don't touch the wound, it could get infected.) Do not confuse it with infester, to infest.
Feminine: la pécheresse. Careful: le pêcheur with the circumflex is the fisherman.

Allier qc à qc means to combine one thing with another. Ce plat allie la douceur du miel à l'acidité du citron. (This dish combines the sweetness of honey with the sourness of lemon.) Reflexively, s'allier à qn means to ally oneself with someone.
It refers to the recent past, not to being last in a series, which would be en dernier. Dernièrement, je n'ai pas eu le temps de lire. (Lately, I have not had time to read.)
Nouns ending in té are feminine. Common: parler avec fermeté.
Used only in the plural and feminine: de longues fiançailles. The related verb is se fiancer avec qn.
Word family: lent, lentement, ralentir, le ralentissement.
lent is the adjective and agrees with its noun: la connexion est lente, le train est lent. lentement is the adverb and does not fit here.
French keeps adjective and adverb strictly apart: a verb needs the adverb lentement, never lent.

cards.de: Slow down, there's a bend ahead!
cards.note: The tu imperative keeps the -s here: ralentis, not ralenti. The plural form is ralentissez !

cards.de: The train slowed down as it came into the station.
cards.answer: Le train a ralenti en entrant en gare.
accept: Le train a ralenti quand il est entré en gare.
cards.note: ralentir on its own expresses the process of getting slower, so there is no need for devenir plus lent.

cards.de: There is slow-moving traffic on the motorway.
cards.fr: Il y a des ___ sur l'autoroute.
cards.note: In traffic contexts le ralentissement means a hold-up or stretch of slow traffic. Traffic reports nearly always use the plural: des ralentissements.

cards.task: Rewrite using the adverb lentement, with il as the subject.
cards.note: Adjective plus noun can often be turned into verb plus adverb. The adverb is built from the feminine form lente plus -ment.
escargot is masculine, so the adjective is lents. Learn all four forms: lent, lente, lents, lentes.

cards.de: Can you speak more slowly, please?
cards.answer: Tu peux parler plus lentement, s'il te plaît ?
accept: Peux-tu parler plus lentement, s'il te plaît ?
Tu peux parler moins vite, s'il te plaît ?
cards.note: Adverbs form the comparative with plus: plus lentement. There is no single-word form like lentementer.
English has one verb know, French has two. connaître is for people, places and things you are familiar with; savoir is for facts and skills: je sais nager, je sais où il habite.

cards.de: I am taking you to the cinema.
cards.note: mener is used for people, porter for things. em- means take away from here (emmener, emporter), a- means bring here (amener, apporter).
English has only day, but French splits it: journée is the day as a stretch of time you live through, jour is the unit or the date. Same pairs: an/année, soir/soirée, matin/matinée.

cards.de: Do you know where he lives?
cards.note: English has one verb know, French has two. Use savoir before a clause (où, que, si, comment); connaître always takes a direct noun.

cards.de: The last few years have been difficult.
cards.note: When the year is described or felt as a stretch of time, use année: une année difficile, toute l'année.
English can covers both ability and possibility. A learned skill takes savoir + infinitive; pouvoir would only mean you are free to play right now.

cards.de: I have known her for a long time.
cards.note: People are always known with connaître. savoir is for facts and skills, never for a person.
The prefix em- means take away from here, a- means bring to that place. English take hides this difference.

cards.de: I am getting home at eight tonight.
cards.fr: Ce soir, je ___ à huit heures.
cards.note: rentrer means go back home. revenir is come back to where the speaker is, retourner is go back to that other place.
revenir means come back to where the speaker is, so retourner does not work in this invitation.
English day is both jour and journée. Use journée for the day as a lived stretch of time, jour for the unit or the date: trois jours, quel jour ?
A false friend: it does not mean eventually. It means possibly or if necessary: éventuellement, je peux venir.
Masculine despite the -ée ending, like le musée: aller au lycée. Students there are des lycéens et des lycéennes.
False friend: assister à means be present at. To assist someone is aider quelqu'un.
Formed from librairie. A librarian is un bibliothécaire, which is a different job.

cards.de: I studied at the library all day.
cards.fr: J'ai étudié à la librairie toute la journée.
cards.answer: J'ai étudié à la bibliothèque toute la journée.
cards.note: You cannot study in a librairie, which is a shop. The study place is la bibliothèque.
Here librairie is correct because books are being sold. Keep bibliothèque for collections you consult or borrow from.

cards.de: My daughter works at the university library.
cards.fr: Ma fille travaille à la librairie de l'université.
cards.answer: Ma fille travaille à la bibliothèque de l'université.
cards.note: Classic false friend: librairie means bookshop, while the place with borrowable books is la bibliothèque.

cards.de: After the library, he wants to buy a book at the bookshop.
cards.answer: Après la bibliothèque, il veut acheter un livre à la librairie.
cards.note: Keep the pair straight: bibliothèque for library, librairie for bookshop.

cards.de: With that remark he deeply hurt his colleague.
cards.answer: Avec cette remarque, il a profondément blessé son collègue.
cards.note: Blesser covers emotional hurt as well as physical injury. Never use it for blessing, which is bénir.

cards.fr: Le chien a blessé cet enfant.
cards.task: Put the sentence into the passive.
cards.answer: Cet enfant a été blessé par le chien.
cards.note: Blesser means to injure, so the passive says the child was injured, not blessed. In the passive, être plus the participle agrees with the subject.
Not the English allure, which is le charme or la séduction. Common phrases: à toute allure (at full speed), avoir de l'allure (to look stylish).
La drogue only means narcotics. The drug you get from a pharmacy is un médicament.
Masculine: le coffre. It is also the boot of a car, and le coffre-fort is a safe.
Placed before the noun, un brave homme means a good sort, not a courageous one. After the noun, un homme brave does mean brave.
Not the English essence (l'essentiel, la nature). Faire le plein d'essence means to fill up the tank.

User does not mean to use, which is utiliser or se servir de. Tu vas user tes chaussures si tu cours avec. (You'll wear out your shoes if you run in them.) S'user means to wear out, and user de qc means to make use of something.
Le bal is only the dance. The ball you throw or kick is une balle or un ballon.
Un préservatif is never a food preservative, which is un conservateur. A famous trap on ingredient labels.
Feminine: une pipe, as in fumer la pipe. Not to be confused with le tuyau, the pipe that carries water.
Do not reach for familier, which means informal or over familiar. Plural of familial is familiaux.
Masculine: un bon cavalier; the feminine is une cavalière. Nouns in -ier such as le pompier and le policier are masculine.
Not the English emission of gases. Une émission de télévision is a TV show.
Feminine: la jalousie, like other nouns in -ie (la folie, la maladie). From the adjective jaloux, jalouse.

cards.de: the lower secondary school (ages 11 to 15 in France)
cards.note: False friend: le collège is not a college or university. Higher education is l'université, and after le collège comes le lycée.
False friend: une blouse is a work coat or smock worn by doctors and schoolchildren. A woman's blouse is un chemisier.
Masculine: un coup de canon. Same -on ending as le poumon and le camion; in familiar speech, c'est canon means it looks stunning.
La médecine is only the field of study. A medicine you swallow is un médicament, and the doctor is le médecin.
False friend: it means once and for all, not definitely in the sense of certainly. For that use certainement or sans aucun doute.
False friend: rester does not mean to rest, which is se reposer. Je préfère rester à la maison ce soir. (I'd rather stay home tonight.)

cards.de: the detached family house (in the suburbs)
cards.note: False friend: un pavillon is an ordinary suburban house with a garden, not a sports pavilion or a tent. A second meaning is a ship's flag.

cards.de: slender, tiny (of a person or of small tasks)
cards.note: As an adjective menu, menue means fine, slight or small: une femme menue (a slight woman), de menus travaux (small jobs). The set meal is le menu, a noun.

False friend: it confirms what someone said and does not mean effectively. Effectivement, tu as raison sur ce point. (Indeed, you are right about that.) Effectively in the sense of efficiently is efficacement.
False friend: le pétrole is oil in the ground, not petrol for your car, which is l'essence.

cards.de: the secret you tell someone in private
cards.note: False friend: confidence in the sense of trust is la confiance. Typical use: faire des confidences à quelqu'un.

cards.de: to take on, to accept (responsibility, consequences)
cards.note: False friend: assumer never means to assume in the sense of suppose, which is supposer. Il doit assumer les conséquences de son choix. (He has to accept the consequences of his choice.) Typical use: assumer ses responsabilités.
False friend: une remarque spirituelle is a witty remark, not a spiritual one. The feminine form is spirituelle.
False friend: une manifestation is usually a street protest. Informally it is la manif, and the verb is manifester.
False friend: un slip is underwear for men or women, not a slip worn under a dress, which is une combinaison. Note that it is masculine.
False friend: la fantaisie means a whim or playfulness, as in agir selon sa fantaisie. English fantasy in the sense of imagination is l'imagination, and a daydream is un fantasme.

cards.de: the court hearing (session before a judge)
cards.note: Une audience is usually a hearing in court, or viewing figures in the media. The people watching a show are le public or les spectateurs.

cards.de: moving, deeply touching (a scene, a speech)
cards.note: Pathétique normally means moving or poignant, not pathetic. For the dismissive English sense use lamentable or minable.

cards.de: the box (small square to tick on a form)
cards.note: La case is a box or square on a form or board: cocher une case. An English case is le cas, or une valise for luggage.

cards.de: the death throes (final struggle before dying)
cards.note: L'agonie refers to actually dying: être à l'agonie. English agony meaning severe pain is une douleur atroce.
La balance is a weighing machine. Balance in the sense of steadiness is l'équilibre, and a bank balance is le solde.
In a restaurant you ask L'addition, s'il vous plait. Addition in the sense of something added is un ajout.
Éventuel means possible or potential, not eventual. Feminine éventuelle; éventuellement means possibly, while eventually is finalement or en fin de compte.
Masculine, like other job words in -ier: le pompier, le policier, le douanier. A feminine form exists too: une brigadière.
Not a comedian: un comédien plays any role, including tragic ones. A comedian who tells jokes is un humoriste or un comique. Feminine: la comédienne.

cards.de: the jacket (of a suit or worn over a shirt)
cards.note: False friend: une veste is a jacket, not a vest. A waistcoat is un gilet and an undershirt is un maillot de corps.

cards.de: to claim (to say something that may not be true)
cards.note: Not to pretend: prétendre means to claim. Il prétend connaître le directeur personnellement. (He claims to know the director personally.) To pretend as in play acting is faire semblant.
Feminine: la boue, like la roue and la joue. Adjective boueux, boueuse: un chemin boueux.

cards.de: the congratulation (usually said in the plural)
cards.note: Feminine: la félicitation, and every noun in -tion is feminine. You almost always hear the plural: Félicitations !
Masculine: un rouleau de scotch, scotcher une affiche au mur. The same word also means Scotch whisky.

cards.de: the starter, the first course of a meal
cards.note: In France une entrée comes before the main course, unlike the American entrée. The main course is le plat principal.
Nothing to do with blessing: blesser means to hurt physically or emotionally. Tes paroles ont vraiment blessé ta sœur. (Your words really hurt your sister.) To bless is bénir.
Not a romance or anything Roman: un roman is any novel. Ancient Roman is romain and romantic is romantique.
Looks like the English word smoking but means formal evening wear. Smoking as an activity is fumer or le tabagisme.

cards.de: the rank (in the army or police)
cards.note: Masculine, despite the ending -ade, which is usually feminine (la salade, la promenade). Useful phrase: monter en grade.

cards.de: the activist, the committed party member
cards.note: Not militant in the English sense of aggressive: un militant écologiste is simply an environmental campaigner. Feminine: une militante.
Masculine: un châle en laine, se couvrir les épaules d'un châle. Note the circumflex on the a.
Do not say je suis excité for looking forward to something: with people it often suggests sexual arousal. Use impatient or enthousiaste instead.
Masculine: le canot, like other nouns in -ot such as le pot and le chariot. Un canot de sauvetage is a lifeboat.
Feminine: la franchise, like most nouns in -ise (la bêtise, la surprise). Say something en toute franchise, in all honesty.

cards.de: the sentence handed down by a court, the verdict
cards.note: Not a sentence in grammar, which is la phrase. La sentence is a judgment and can also mean a maxim.
Feminine: une lueur. Like chaleur, douleur and peur, it ends in -eur and is feminine; common in une lueur d'espoir, a glimmer of hope.
Not a palace, which is le palais. Un palace is a five star hotel.
faire attention à qc means to pay attention to something or watch out for it.
French says avoir raison, literally to have right, where English uses to be right. No article after the verb.

cards.fr: Je crois que tu es tort.
cards.answer: Je crois que tu as tort.
cards.note: The opposite of avoir raison also uses avoir: avoir tort. Neither phrase takes an article.

cards.de: Keep an eye on the children!
cards.note: The pattern is faire attention à qn/qc. Before a plural, à + les contracts to aux.
You say poser une question, never demander une question. Add the person with à: poser une question à quelqu'un.

cards.de: I feel like going to the cinema.
cards.note: avoir envie de + infinitive expresses wanting or fancying something. As with avoir raison, there is no article.
The fixed phrase is faire attention à. prendre attention does not exist in French.

cards.fr: Il prend des progrès en français.
cards.answer: Il fait des progrès en français.
cards.note: To make progress is faire des progrès. prendre only works with words like décision, rendez-vous and notes.

cards.fr: Il faut faire attention à cette règle.
cards.task: Rewrite as an imperative with tu.
cards.note: Faire keeps its s in the tu imperative: fais. The à stays in place before the object.
After avoir, peur takes no article: j'ai peur des chiens. The preposition is de, never devant.

cards.de: to feel down, to have the blues
cards.note: le cafard literally means cockroach. Avoir le cafard means to feel sad or low.

cards.de: to stand someone up (not turn up to a meeting)
cards.note: The person is always introduced by à, as an indirect object. You never say poser quelqu'un un lapin.

cards.de: Since he left, I have been feeling sad.
cards.note: The idiom always takes the definite article: avoir le cafard. Un cafard would be a real insect.

cards.fr: Ce voyage coûte les yeux de tête.
cards.answer: Ce voyage coûte les yeux de la tête.
cards.note: The article la before tête cannot be dropped. The phrase is fixed: les yeux de la tête.

cards.de: The new bike cost a fortune.
cards.answer: Le nouveau vélo a coûté les yeux de la tête.
accept: Le nouveau vélo m'a coûté les yeux de la tête.
cards.note: Coûter forms its passé composé with avoir, and the idiom itself stays unchanged.

cards.fr: Il a posé un lapin à Julie.
cards.answer: Il lui a posé un lapin.
cards.note: Because the person is linked with à, you need the indirect pronoun lui. La would be wrong here.

cards.de: Have you stood me up again?
cards.answer: Tu m'as encore posé un lapin ?
accept: Tu m'as encore une fois posé un lapin ?
Est-ce que tu m'as encore posé un lapin ?
cards.note: The pronoun me comes before the auxiliary. Encore here carries the sense of yet again.

cards.de: He stood me up on Saturday.
cards.fr: Il m'___ posé un lapin samedi.
cards.note: Poser is a transitive verb, so its passé composé takes avoir. The auxiliary is never être here, even with the pronoun m'.

cards.fr: Ce sac coûte les yeux de la tête.
cards.answer: Ce sac a coûté les yeux de la tête.
cards.note: Coûter is conjugated with avoir and the participle stays invariable.
la bagnole and la caisse are colloquial. la voiture is neutral, while le véhicule sounds official.
In speech tu es often contracts to t'es. Leaving the question word at the end is everyday spoken style; inversion sounds formal.

Bouffer is slang and fine among friends, but out of place with strangers or in a restaurant. On va bouffer un kebab après le film ? (Shall we grab a kebab after the film?) Neutral is manger, formal se nourrir.

cards.de: The doctor explains how to eat properly.
cards.note: se nourrir belongs to a formal or technical register and fits medicine and nutrition. bouffer would be far too slangy here.

cards.fr: Y a personne dans la rue.
cards.answer: Il n'y a personne dans la rue.
cards.note: In speech the il of il y a is often dropped, and the ne of the negation disappears too. In writing you need il n'y a.
chuis is the spoken contraction of je suis, and crevé is the slangy version of fatigué. Write either one only when you want to show casual speech.

cards.de: Hello, Mr Director, I would like an appointment.
cards.fr: Salut Monsieur le Directeur, je voudrais un rendez-vous.
cards.answer: Bonjour Monsieur le Directeur, je voudrais un rendez-vous.
accept: Bonjour Monsieur le Directeur, je voudrais obtenir un rendez-vous.
cards.note: salut is only for friends and people you say tu to. In formal situations it is always bonjour.

cards.de: Hello, I would like a starter.
cards.fr: Bonjour, je voudrais bouffer une entrée.
cards.answer: Bonjour, je voudrais prendre une entrée.
accept: Bonjour, je vais prendre une entrée.
cards.note: In a restaurant you use prendre, or just je voudrais. bouffer is closer to "to scoff" and sounds rude to staff.

cards.de: I don't feel like working. (casual spoken French)
cards.note: In everyday speech the ne is almost always dropped. bosser is the colloquial version of travailler.
le boulot and le taf are colloquial, le travail is neutral, and l'emploi belongs in contracts and statistics.
le fric and le pognon are slang for money. les espèces means cash in banking language, and la monnaie is loose change.

cards.fr: Il ne sait pas ce qu'il veut.
cards.task: Turn it into casual spoken French.
cards.answer: Il sait pas ce qu'il veut.
cards.note: In everyday spoken French the ne disappears and pas alone carries the negation. In written texts the ne stays.
s'est = se + est, used with reflexive verbs. c'est = it is, ses = his/her, ces = these.

Son and est are easy to hear but the verbs are the ones that change: sont is the plural of être with mes cousins, est the singular with il. Note ces (those children, pointing) versus ses (her parents, possession), a pair learners mix up most often.

The accent marks the word that is not a verb form or conjunction: à (preposition) against a (from avoir), où (place) against ou ("or"). In the last two, ce sits before a noun while se belongs to the reflexive verb se lever.
où means where or where to, while ou means or. It is the only French word written with ù.
a without an accent is the verb form of avoir. Test: you can replace it with avait, elle avait vingt ans.
The preposition à always carries an accent. Only the verb form a from avoir goes without one.

cards.de: I don't know what time it is.
cards.fr: Je ne sais pas ___ heure il est.
cards.note: quel/quelle is a question word and agrees with its noun. heure is feminine, so quelle.

cards.task: Turn it into an indirect question, starting with: Je me demande ...
cards.answer: Je me demande quelle est ton adresse.
accept: Je me demande quelle est ton adresse .
cards.note: In an indirect question quelle is still the question word. qu'elle would be wrong here, because no clause with elle as subject follows.

cards.de: He forgot his keys at home.
cards.fr: Il a oublié ___ clés à la maison.
cards.note: ses is the plural possessive, his or her. ces means these or those.
c'est = ce + est and means "that is". s'est only ever belongs to a reflexive verb, for example il s'est levé.
ces is the plural of ce/cette and means "these". Don't confuse it with ses, which means "his" or "her".
Before the verb, leur is the pronoun meaning "to them" and never takes an s. The possessive leur is the one that can become leurs.

cards.de: The day we met was a Sunday.
cards.answer: Le jour où nous nous sommes rencontrés était un dimanche.
accept: Le jour où on s'est rencontrés était un dimanche.
cards.note: où covers not just places but also points in time, as in le jour où or le moment où. English often uses "when" or nothing at all here.
Before a vowel or a silent h the e drops out: l'homme, j'aime, qu'il. This does not happen with h aspiré: le héros.
With h aspiré there is no elision and no liaison: la haine, le héros, le hasard. Only a silent h allows elision: l'heure, l'hôtel.

cards.fr: Je me demande s'elle est d'accord.
cards.answer: Je me demande si elle est d'accord.
cards.note: s'elle does not exist. The elision of si applies to il and ils only.

accept: Vous avez deux heures de temps.
cards.note: In vous avez and deux heures the s and the x are pronounced [z] and linked to the next word. After pronouns and numbers the liaison is obligatory.
ne also elides before a vowel: n'ai, n'est, n'ont. The negation is still complete, with pas or rien after the verb.

cards.fr: Je ne aime pas que il parte si tôt.
cards.task: Rewrite with all the necessary elisions.
cards.answer: Je n'aime pas qu'il parte si tôt.
cards.note: ne, que, je, me, te, se, ce, de and la lose their vowel before another vowel. The apostrophe replaces it with no space after it.

cards.de: the peach (also the activity of fishing)
cards.note: Feminine, and the same word covers both the fruit and fishing. Say: aller à la pêche.
Masculine: le viol est un crime. Do not confuse it with la violence or le violon, the instrument.

cards.de: She lives on a small pension.
cards.note: A retirement pension is la retraite. Une pension in French is more often a boarding house or board and lodging.
cards.hint: Same word as the word for retirement.

cards.de: I bought this novel at the bookshop.
cards.fr: J'ai acheté ce roman à la ___.
cards.note: La librairie is a bookshop; a library is la bibliothèque.
cards.hint: Not the place where you borrow books.

cards.de: I actually live in Lyon at the moment.
cards.note: Actuellement means currently, not actually. For actually in the sense of in reality, use en fait.
cards.hint: Think of the time, not of the truth.

cards.note: Assister à qch means to attend. J'ai assisté à une conférence très intéressante hier. (I attended a very interesting lecture yesterday.) To assist someone is aider quelqu'un.
cards.hint: Looks like to assist, takes the preposition à.

cards.note: Masculine, like other nouns in -age: le voyage, le fromage, le paysage. Often used in the plural: faire ses bagages.
Feminine, like all nouns in -sion: la décision, la télévision. In the plural, les provisions means the food shopping.
Feminine, like other nouns in -esse: la promesse, la vitesse, la tristesse. Well known phrase: la messe de minuit.
Feminine: la clef, an older spelling of la clé, both pronounced the same. Also used figuratively: le mot clef, the key word.
Attendre already contains the for: j'attends mon frère. Never say attendre pour someone.
Chercher means to look for, so no pour or à follows. Same with écouter la musique, no to.
Masculine: le golf, jouer au golf, un terrain de golf. Watch out for le golfe with an e, which is a bay in the sea.
Masculine: un gang de malfaiteurs. Borrowed words like un gang, un club, un test are almost always masculine; note une bande for a looser group of friends.
Masculine: un boy, a borrowing kept as it is, plural des boys. It also names a male dancer in a revue.
Visiter is for places (visiter un musée). For people use rendre visite à or aller voir.
Connaître is for people and places you are familiar with; savoir is for facts and skills.
cards.hint: The verb for being acquainted with.

cards.de: I have been learning French for two years.
cards.note: Use an after a number; année stresses duration or quality, as in une année difficile.
cards.hint: A counted number takes the short form.

cards.de: Can you bring the cake to the party?
cards.note: Apporter is for things you carry; amener and emmener are for people you accompany. Est-ce que tu peux apporter le gâteau à la fête ? (Can you bring the cake to the party?)
cards.fr: Tu peux ___ le gâteau à la fête ?
cards.hint: The object is a thing, not a person.

cards.note: Masculine: un artifice, like le service and le sacrifice. Best known in un feu d'artifice, a fireworks display.
Masculine, like le paysan and l'artisan. Common use: je suis partisan d'une solution simple.

cards.de: The situation has become difficult over the last few months.
cards.fr: ___ situation est devenue difficile ces derniers mois.
cards.note: Every noun ending in -tion is feminine: la situation, la question, la solution. There are no exceptions.

cards.de: The temperature dropped by five degrees last night.
cards.fr: ___ température a baissé de cinq degrés cette nuit.
cards.note: Nouns ending in -ure are feminine, including the many words in -ture: la température, la lecture, la peinture.
Nouns ending in -e look feminine to learners, but le problème, le système and le thème are all masculine. Plural: les problèmes.

cards.de: the ridiculousness (absurdity, the quality of being laughable)
cards.note: Masculine: le ridicule. Famous in le ridicule ne tue pas, ridicule does not kill. The same word also works as an adjective, c'est ridicule.

cards.de: Yesterday we visited the Eiffel Tower.
cards.note: La tour means tower and is feminine. Le tour means a walk, a turn or an order of play.

cards.de: After the meal we always take a little walk around the neighbourhood.
cards.fr: Après le repas, nous faisons toujours ___ petit tour dans le quartier.
cards.note: Faire un tour means to go for a stroll or a short walk. Here tour is masculine, unlike la tour (the tower).

cards.de: She has found a new position (job) in Lyon.
cards.fr: Elle a trouvé ___ nouveau poste à Lyon.
cards.note: In the sense of a job, poste is masculine: un poste de professeur. The post office, however, is la poste.

cards.de: She has to hand in her master's thesis in June.
cards.fr: Elle doit rendre ___ mémoire de master en juin.
cards.note: Un mémoire de master is masculine, so son mémoire. With la mémoire (memory) you would say sa mémoire.

cards.de: In summer we go sailing on the Breton coast.
cards.fr: En été, nous faisons de ___ voile sur la côte bretonne.
cards.note: La voile is a sail, and faire de la voile means to go sailing. Le voile is a veil.

cards.de: I read the newspapers every morning.
cards.note: Nouns ending in -al usually form the plural in -aux: le journal, les journaux.

cards.fr: Les ___ de la ville sont surchargés.
cards.note: hôpital → hôpitaux, just like journal → journaux. The circumflex stays in place.

cards.de: I have to change the tyres before winter.
cards.fr: Je dois changer les ___ avant l'hiver.
cards.note: Nouns in -eu usually take -x (les jeux, les feux), but pneu and bleu simply take -s.

cards.de: Prices have gone up this year.
cards.note: Nouns ending in -s, -x or -z do not change in the plural: le prix, les prix, le nez, les nez.

cards.fr: Un kilo ___ tomates, s'il vous plaît.
cards.note: After measures and containers like un kilo, un litre, une bouteille or une tranche, use de with no article after it.

cards.de: She works as a waitress in a café in the centre.
cards.fr: Elle travaille comme ___ dans un café du centre.
cards.note: serveur becomes serveuse. The same pattern gives coiffeur, coiffeuse and vendeur, vendeuse.
Before a vowel or silent h, the masculine forms are vieil, bel and nouvel. The feminine forms are vieille, belle, nouvelle.
sec → sèche. Similar cases: frais → fraîche, blanc → blanche.
Before a vowel the masculine form beau becomes bel. So un bel arbre, but un beau jardin.
Before a vowel nouveau becomes nouvel, so two vowel sounds do not clash. The same happens with bel and vieil.

cards.de: I often talk to the old lady.
cards.note: The feminine of vieux is vieille, with a double l. The form vieil is only used before masculine nouns starting with a vowel.
The masculine plural of beau is beaux, even before a vowel. bel is never used in the plural.
Before the noun, propre means own. After the noun it means clean: une voiture propre.

cards.de: He is a poor man (I feel sorry for him), I pity him.
cards.note: Before the noun, pauvre expresses pity. After the noun it means having no money.

cards.de: My dear colleague, that is not true.
cards.fr: Mon ___ collègue, ce n'est pas vrai.
cards.note: Before the noun, cher means dear, often when addressing someone. After the noun it means expensive.
Before the noun, seul means only or single. After the noun it means alone or lonely.

cards.de: I have read more than ten books.
cards.note: Use plus de before numbers and quantities. Nothing is being compared here, a quantity is simply being stated.

cards.de: He works more than his brother.
cards.note: When two people or things are compared, use plus que. Only before numbers and quantities do you say plus de.

cards.de: I have less time than you.
cards.note: Before a noun you use moins de with no article. The second part of the comparison is then introduced by que.

cards.de: He has as many friends as I do.
cards.note: An equal quantity is autant de, shortened to autant d' before a vowel. With adjectives and adverbs you use aussi ... que instead.

cards.de: The weather is getting worse and worse.
cards.note: French builds this kind of increase with de ... en ...: de mieux en mieux means better and better. It usually goes with aller or être.
-ent becomes -emment and -ant becomes -amment: constant → constamment. Both endings sound the same, [amɑ̃].
Adjectives ending in -ent form the adverb with -emment: prudent → prudemment, différent → différemment.
Adjectives ending in -ant change to -amment: courant → couramment, constant → constamment. The ending is pronounced [amɑ̃].
The normal pattern is the feminine form of the adjective plus -ment: heureuse → heureusement, douce → doucement.
A few adverbs add an é before the ending: profondément, précisément. absolument, however, has no accent.
The fixed order is me/te/se/nous/vous, then le/la/les, then lui/leur, then y, then en. English word order is no guide here.

cards.de: I do not understand this rule either.
cards.fr: ___, je ne comprends pas cette règle.
cards.note: Short answers with no verb need a stressed pronoun: moi aussi for me too and moi non plus for me neither.

cards.de: I think our neighbours are very nice.
cards.fr: Je trouve que ___ sont très sympathiques.
cards.note: notre goes before a singular noun, nos before a plural one. The ending says nothing about the gender of the noun.
quelque chose, rien and personne take de plus a masculine adjective: rien de grave, personne d'important.
In the passé composé, personne comes after the past participle: je n'ai vu personne. It lands right at the end of the sentence.
In the passé composé, rien goes before the participle while personne goes after it. Compare: je n'ai rien vu, je n'ai vu personne.

cards.de: Each of us made a mistake.
cards.fr: ___ d'entre nous a fait une erreur.
cards.note: chacun d'entre nous means each of us, and the verb stays singular.

cards.de: I prefer to take the train.
cards.note: In préférer the second é becomes è when the ending is silent: je préfère, ils préfèrent. But nous préférons.

cards.de: Next year I'll buy a new car.
cards.fr: L'année prochaine, j'___ une nouvelle voiture.
cards.note: In the futur and the conditionnel the è stays in every form: j'achèterai, nous achèterions.

cards.de: I take an Italian course in the evenings.
cards.fr: Je ___ un cours d'italien le soir.
cards.note: je suis can come from être or from suivre. In French you "follow" a course: suivre un cours.
The participle of prendre is pris. Likewise: apprendre, appris; comprendre, compris.
The participle of ouvrir is ouvert. Likewise: offrir, offert; découvrir, découvert.

cards.de: He wrote me an email yesterday.
cards.note: The participle of écrire is écrit. Likewise: décrire, décrit; dire, dit.
être forms its passé composé with avoir, and the participle is été: j'ai été.
venir takes être and its participle is venu. With a feminine plural subject you add es: venues.

cards.de: I haven't seen the film yet.
cards.note: In the passé composé the negation wraps around the auxiliary: ne ... pas before the participle. The word encore follows after it.
The imparfait stem comes from nous savons: sav-.

cards.de: We used to eat at my grandmother's every Sunday.
cards.fr: Nous ___ tous les dimanches chez ma grand-mère.
cards.note: Verbs in -ger only add the extra e before a and o, so je mangeais but nous mangions.

cards.de: It was cold and it was raining.
cards.note: The stem comes from nous faisons: fais-. Descriptions of past weather are almost always in the imparfait.

cards.de: I was reading when the phone rang.
cards.fr: Je ___ quand le téléphone a sonné.
cards.note: The imparfait sets the ongoing background, while the passé composé gives the sudden event.

cards.de: Shall we go to the cinema?
cards.note: Si plus the imparfait makes a suggestion in French, like How about going ...? or Shall we ...?

cards.de: To be about to do something means being ready to do it right away.
cards.fr: ___, c'est être prêt à le faire tout de suite.
cards.answer: être sur le point de faire quelque chose
cards.note: This expression is even more immediate than the futur proche. It is always followed by de plus an infinitive.

cards.de: It would have been better to wait a bit longer.
cards.note: The set phrase il vaut mieux appears here in the conditionnel passé: il aurait mieux valu plus infinitive. The subject il is impersonal and never changes.

cards.de: I want you to be happy.
cards.note: être has an irregular subjonctif: que je sois, que tu sois, que nous soyons, qu'ils soient. vouloir que always takes the subjonctif.

cards.de: I'm explaining it to you so that you understand.
cards.fr: Je te l'explique pour que tu ___.
cards.note: pour que and afin que always take the subjonctif. comprendre: que je comprenne, que nous comprenions.

cards.de: I'm surprised that he wants to leave so early.
cards.fr: Je suis étonné qu'il ___ partir si tôt.
cards.note: Expressions of feeling such as être étonné que, être content que or c'est dommage que require the subjonctif. vouloir: que je veuille, que nous voulions.

cards.fr: Je suis content que tu ___ venu.
cards.note: The subjonctif passé is the auxiliary in the subjonctif plus the past participle. Feelings trigger the subjonctif.

cards.de: It's a shame that she didn't phone.
cards.note: The negation wraps around the auxiliary only: qu'elle n'ait pas téléphoné. The participle follows it.

cards.de: You have to be finished before midday.
cards.fr: Il faut que tu ___ terminé avant midi.
cards.note: Here the subjonctif passé marks an action that must be completed by a later point in time, like English "have finished by".

cards.de: I could see he was sad, even though he said nothing.
cards.fr: J'ai bien vu qu'il était triste, ___.
cards.note: bien que takes the subjonctif, here the subjonctif passé for an earlier action. With rien and jamais too, the second negative word comes straight after the auxiliary: n'ait rien dit.
vouloir only has the polite imperative forms veuille/veuillez. Veuillez plus infinitive is the formal way to ask for something.
The nous form of the imperative is the present tense without the pronoun. It corresponds to English "Let's ...".

cards.de: Know that I'm always here for you.
cards.fr: ___ que je suis toujours là pour toi.
cards.note: The imperative of savoir is sache. It is often used with que plus a clause.
Normally the form is mange with no -s, but the -s comes back before en and y: manges-en, penses-y.

cards.de: Where is the dress that you bought?
cards.fr: Où est la robe que tu as ___ ?
cards.note: The direct object que comes before the verb and refers to la robe (feminine singular). With avoir, the participle only agrees with a direct object that precedes it.

cards.de: We wrote to each other for years.
cards.fr: Nous nous sommes ___ pendant des années.
cards.note: écrire à quelqu'un takes an indirect object. When se is indirect, there is no agreement.

cards.de: The post is delivered every morning at nine o'clock.
cards.fr: Le courrier ___ chaque matin à neuf heures.
cards.note: The French present passive is être in the present plus the past participle. Use être where English uses "is/are".

cards.de: I realised that it was late.
cards.fr: Je ___ rendu compte qu'il était tard.
cards.note: se rendre compte means to realise. rendu never changes because compte is the direct object: elle s'est rendu compte.
s'en aller means to go away or leave. The reflexive pronoun and en both come before the verb: je m'en vais, tu t'en vas, il s'en va.

cards.de: I have to leave straight away.
cards.note: Even in the infinitive, the reflexive pronoun matches the subject: je dois m'en aller, nous devons nous en aller.

cards.fr: Elle s'est rendu compte ___ son erreur.
cards.note: Before a noun you use se rendre compte de, before a clause se rendre compte que.
In the affirmative imperative the pronoun comes first, then en, all joined by hyphens: allez-vous-en.

cards.de: I only found out the truth yesterday.
cards.fr: C'est seulement hier que j'___ la vérité.
cards.note: In the passé composé savoir means to find out, a single moment. In the imparfait (je savais) it simply means to know.

cards.de: I have already seen this film three times.
cards.note: A countable number of repetitions (trois fois) is a completed fact, so the passé composé is used. Only vague habits take the imparfait.

cards.de: If I had time, I would come.
cards.fr: Si j'___ le temps, je viendrais.
cards.note: si + imparfait, with the main clause in the conditionnel. The conditionnel never follows si.

cards.de: If you come tomorrow, we will go to the cinema.
cards.fr: Si tu ___ demain, nous irons au cinéma.
cards.note: For real conditions, si is followed by the présent, never the future, just as English says if you come and not if you will come. The main clause takes the futur simple.

cards.de: If it rains, we stay at home.
cards.fr: ___ pleut, nous restons à la maison.
cards.note: Before il and ils, si becomes s'. Before elle, on and nous it stays si: si elle veut, si on part.

cards.de: If you are cold, close the window.
cards.fr: Si tu as froid, ___ la fenêtre.
cards.note: After si + présent, the main clause can also be an imperative or a present tense, not only a future.

cards.de: If I had accepted that job, I would be living in Lyon today.
cards.fr: Si j'avais accepté ce poste, j'___ à Lyon aujourd'hui.
cards.note: Mixed type: the condition is in the past (plus-que-parfait) but the result applies today, so the conditionnel présent is used.

cards.de: If you (plural) had arrived on time, you would have seen the beginning of the film.
cards.fr: Si vous étiez arrivés à l'heure, vous ___ le début du film.
cards.note: The main clause takes the conditionnel passé: aurais, aurais, aurait, aurions, auriez, auraient plus the participle. The participle of voir is vu.

cards.de: She acts as if she doesn't know me.
cards.fr: Elle fait comme si elle ne me ___ pas.
cards.note: Comme si always takes the imparfait or the plus-que-parfait, never the présent or the conditionnel. English can say as if she doesn't know, but French shifts the tense back.

cards.de: I would come more often if I lived closer.
cards.fr: Je ___ plus souvent si j'habitais plus près.
cards.note: The si clause can also come second; the sequence of tenses stays the same. The conditionnel stem of venir is viendr-.

cards.de: She talks as if she knew everything.
cards.note: comme si is never followed by the présent, futur or conditionnel: use the imparfait (same time) or the plus-que-parfait (earlier). Before il and ils, si becomes s': comme s'il dormait.

cards.de: We are leaving tomorrow, unless the weather is bad.
cards.fr: Nous partons demain, à moins qu'il ___ mauvais.
cards.note: à moins que means unless and takes the subjonctif, often with the stylistic ne: à moins qu'il ne fasse mauvais.

cards.de: When I am in Paris, I will call you.
cards.fr: Quand je ___ à Paris, je t'appellerai.
cards.note: After quand, French uses the futur for future events, where English keeps the present.
The quand clause takes the futur even when the main clause is an imperative. English uses the present here.

cards.de: As soon as the train arrives, we will call you.
cards.fr: Dès que le train ___, nous t'appellerons.
cards.note: Dès que, aussitôt que and lorsque behave like quand and require the futur.

cards.de: I will write to you as soon as I am in Paris.
cards.fr: Je t'écrirai ___ je serai à Paris.
cards.note: Dès que takes the futur when referring to the future, just like quand. Do not confuse it with si, which introduces a condition.

cards.de: She lets the children play outside.
cards.note: She is only allowing it, so laisser + infinitive. With fait jouer she would be making them play or organising it.
penser à qn/qc means to think of someone or something. penser de qc means to have an opinion: Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ce film ?
arrêter de faire qc.
The set phrase is avoir besoin de qch. Note ton aide: aide is feminine, but ton is used because the word starts with a vowel.

cards.fr: Il n'a pas répondu ___ ma question.
cards.note: répondre à qn or à qch. French adds à where English has a direct object.

cards.de: She managed to find a flat.
cards.fr: Elle a réussi ___ trouver un appartement.
cards.note: réussir à faire qch. It also works with a noun: réussir à un examen means to pass an exam.

cards.de: He is sure he is right.
cards.hint: sûr + preposition, shortened before a vowel
cards.note: sûr de + infinitive says what someone is convinced of. Before a vowel, de becomes d'.

cards.fr: La machine ___ laver est en panne.
cards.note: After a noun, à + infinitive states the purpose: une machine à laver, une machine à écrire. English uses a compound noun instead.

cards.de: I bought a toothbrush for the trip.
cards.note: à dents gives the purpose of the brush. Dents always stays plural here.

cards.de: Put the wine glasses on the table.
cards.fr: Mets les verres ___ vin sur la table.
cards.note: This is about the type of glass, so the purpose: un verre à vin, un verre à eau. Use un verre de vin for a glass with wine in it.

cards.de: My grandmother still has a sewing machine.
cards.note: Again à + infinitive for what the device does. Likewise: une machine à laver, un fer à repasser.
à merges with les to give aux: la boîte aux lettres. Learn this fixed expression as a whole.
Use en with feminine countries (en France), au with masculine ones (au Portugal, au Canada), aux with plurals (aux États-Unis) and à with cities.

cards.de: Next week we are flying to the USA.
cards.fr: La semaine prochaine, nous partons ___ États-Unis.
cards.note: Countries with plural names take aux: aux États-Unis, aux Pays-Bas, aux Philippines.

cards.de: This weekend I am sleeping at my aunt's.
cards.note: chez covers both at someone's place and to someone's place. The verb shows the direction: aller chez or être chez.

cards.de: We are going to Italy by car.
cards.note: Vehicles you get inside take en with no article: en voiture, en train, en bus. Never use avec here for English by.

cards.de: In the morning I walk to work.
cards.fr: Le matin, je vais au travail ___.
cards.note: Use à when you are not enclosed in the vehicle: à pied, à vélo, à cheval. Always without an article.

cards.de: They went to Corsica by boat.
cards.fr: Ils sont allés en Corse ___ bateau.
cards.note: en bateau follows the rule for vehicles you travel inside. But say sur le bateau when you mean the place on board.

cards.de: I am going to Paris by train.
cards.note: en train is the everyday form. par le train sounds formal and appears in timetables or official texts.

cards.de: I did the exercise in ten minutes.
cards.hint: time taken to complete the action
cards.note: en + time says how long something took to complete, just like English in ten minutes. It answers the question: how long did it take?

cards.de: During the holidays I read a lot.
cards.hint: capital letter at the start of the sentence
cards.note: pendant means during and comes before a period of time or an event. It always needs the article before the noun.

cards.de: I worked in Lyon for two years.
cards.note: English "for" with a length of time is pendant in French. It can also simply be left out here: J'ai travaillé deux ans.
Wide streets and open spaces take sur: sur le boulevard, sur l'avenue, sur la place. Only rue is different: dans la rue.

cards.de: I found the information on the internet.
cards.note: French says sur Internet, sur le site, sur Facebook. Internet takes no article.
With page numbers French uses à la page, never sur la page, even though English says "on".

cards.de: The mirror is hanging on the wall.
cards.note: Something hung up is au mur. Sur le mur suggests directly on the wall surface, as with graffiti.

cards.de: The bakery is on the street corner.
cards.fr: La boulangerie est ___ de la rue.
cards.note: "On the corner" is au coin de la rue. Without de la rue, dans le coin means in the neighbourhood.
personne goes after the past participle, while rien goes before it: je n'ai rien vu.
Before an infinitive, ne and pas stay together in front of the verb: Je préfère ne pas venir.

cards.de: The scene is shown in slow motion.
cards.note: au ralenti means in slow motion, and figuratively at a reduced pace: l'usine tourne au ralenti.

cards.de: Are you bringing the cake to the party?
cards.fr: Tu ___ le gâteau à la fête ?
cards.note: French splits what English calls bring: apporter for things you carry, amener for people you accompany. A cake is apporté.
cards.task: Fill in the correct verb form.

cards.de: Every morning I take my daughter to school.
cards.fr: Chaque matin, j'___ ma fille à l'école.
cards.note: Use amener to take a person somewhere and leave them there; emmener means to take someone along with you. Never apporter with people.
cards.task: Fill in the correct verb form.

cards.de: The holiday was so nice that we want to go back to Italy next year.
cards.fr: Les vacances étaient si belles que nous voulons ___ en Italie l'année prochaine.
cards.note: English go back covers three French verbs: retourner (go back to a place away from here), revenir (come back to where I am), rentrer (go back home).

cards.fr: Ma mère part à la ___ l'année prochaine.
cards.note: La retraite looks like retreat but normally means retirement. The set phrase is partir à la retraite, to retire.

cards.de: He was injured in the accident.
cards.note: Blesser means to wound or injure, not to bless. To bless is bénir, and une blessure is a wound.
Feminine: la lutte, from the verb lutter. Used in la lutte contre le racisme and for the sport of wrestling.

cards.de: She made an important decision yesterday.
cards.note: "Make a decision" is prendre une décision. The past participle of prendre is pris.
"Need" is expressed with avoir besoin de. The de is a fixed part of the phrase, including before quantities.
Before a vowel, spoken French shortens tu to t': t'as, t'es, t'avais. In writing it stays tu as.
veuillez is always followed by an infinitive. It belongs to formal register; the neutral version is Asseyez-vous, s'il vous plaît.
Before a verb, leur means "to them" and never changes. Before a noun, leur/leurs means "their" and agrees with the number of the noun.
qu'elle is que + elle, meaning "that she". Test: you can swap elle for il, je pense qu'il a raison.

cards.de: Are you having tea or coffee?
cards.fr: Tu prends du thé ___ du café ?
cards.note: ou without an accent means "or". Test: you can replace it with ou bien.

cards.de: I don't know if he is coming this evening.
cards.fr: Je ne sais pas ___ vient ce soir.
cards.note: si becomes s' only before il and ils. Before elle, on and every other word it stays si.

cards.de: She thinks (that) we/one has to leave earlier.
cards.fr: Elle pense ___ doit partir plus tôt.
cards.note: que drops its e before a vowel: qu'on, qu'il, qu'elle, qu'ils. The same happens with lorsque, puisque and quoique.

cards.de: We stayed until the end of the film.
cards.note: jusque becomes jusqu' before a vowel: jusqu'à, jusqu'ici, jusqu'alors, jusqu'au bout.
When an inverted verb form ends in a vowel, a t is inserted to keep the sound smooth: a-t-il, parle-t-elle, va-t-on.

cards.de: The construction work lasts three months.
cards.note: Nouns in -ail normally just add s (les détails), but travail becomes travaux and vitrail becomes vitraux.

cards.de: My cousin (female) is a singer in a jazz band.
cards.fr: Ma cousine est ___ dans un groupe de jazz.
cards.note: When the noun goes with a verb (chanter), -eur usually becomes -euse: chanteur, chanteuse.
Form the feminine first, then add the plural s: sec, sèche, sèches.

cards.de: the old trees in the garden
cards.note: In the masculine plural vieux stays the same, and a form vieils does not exist. The special form vieil is only for the singular.
When the adjective ends in a vowel, the e drops out: vrai gives vraiment, poli gives poliment, absolu gives absolument.

cards.de: Those who want to come have to sign up.
cards.note: For a mixed or general group of people you use ceux qui, literally those who. celles qui is only for an all female group.

cards.de: Is this phone yours? (speaking to one person you know well)
cards.note: Ownership is often expressed with être à plus a stressed pronoun: à moi, à toi, à lui. You could also say C'est le tien ?

cards.de: Don't listen, he's just talking nonsense.
cards.note: dire n'importe quoi means to talk nonsense. n'importe quoi refers to things, n'importe qui to people.
e becomes è before a silent ending: j'achète, ils achètent. But nous achetons, vous achetez.
The l doubles before a silent ending: j'appelle, ils appellent. But nous appelons.
